Similarly, the CH077 molecular clone acquired three Env mutations (V208A, R577K, and D743N), NC-N27K, and IN-T122I. CH185 acquired and subsequently lost NC-A30T and acquired two Env mutations (A533V and L764M), another NC mutation (NC-D48N), and two IN mutations (IN-E163K and R263K). We did not identify any mutations in the  \(3^{\prime}\)  PPT G-tract region (39-44) in the viral strains tested here. Inactivating mutations in Vpu were also frequently detected, consistent with previous reports from us and others (47, 74, 75). These observations indicate that DTG resistance pathways shown here are independent of viral isolate and cell type. Notably, the identified NC mutations are within the zinc finger domains. Previous studies suggest that the mutation at IN-T122 may contribute to a higher level of resistance to INSTIs when coupled with G140S/Q148H (76, 77). IN-S153Y, E163K, and R263K are reported as low-level DTG resistance or accessory mutations in the Stanford HIV Drug Resistance Database (78). We also detected several additional mutations in other open reading frames including those for RT, PR, Nef, and p6-Gag. However, these mutations were not consistently found across the different selection experiments.

We observed in the PBMC selections that NC and IN mutations often arose together, suggesting that mutations in these two coding regions may work in concert to increase levels of INSTI resistance. To test this hypothesis, we introduced the NC/IN mutations identified in Fig. 5A into the NL4-3 molecular clone and assessed their effect on sensitivity to INSTIs (Fig. 5, D to F). We found that IN-S153Y and IN-S153Y/D167H conferred 3.4-fold and 2.6-fold resistance to DTG, respectively. NC-N27I alone showed a statistically significant level of resistance to second-generation INSTIs DTG and cabotegravir (CAB) but not to the first-generation INSTI raltegravir (RAL). The level of resistance conferred by the NC-N27I mutation was similar to that of the IN-S153Y and IN-S153Y/D167H mutations. The combination of NC-N27I and IN-S153Y resulted in greater increases in DTG and CAB resistance (8.5-fold and 12.2-fold resistance, respectively) than mutations in either IN or NC alone. Although NC-N27I and IN-S153Y alone did not show statistically significant resistance to RAL, in combination, they conferred a significant level of RAL resistance. While NC-N27I enhanced the resistance conferred by the coselected IN mutations, this NC mutation did not rescue the  \(\sim 2\)  -fold infectivity defect imposed by the IN mutations (Fig. 5G). These results demonstrate that NC and IN mutations that emerge together in PBMCs act in concert to increase INSTI resistance.

## DISCUSSION

In this study, we characterized a panel of NC mutants selected in the presence of DTG. We demonstrated that INSTI resistance conferred by NC mutations is closely associated with accelerated early postentry events in the HIV-1 replication cycle. Notably, while these NC mutations do not have a major effect on virus assembly or infectivity, they significantly shorten the time between completion of reverse transcription/uncoating and viral DNA integration. These results demonstrate that the NC mutations narrow the time window during which INSTIs can effectively inhibit integration, offering a novel mechanism for INSTI resistance.

Unlike canonical HIV-1 drug resistance mutations that directly alter drug-target interactions (33), INSTI resistance mediated by NC mutations must involve alternative mechanisms, as INSTIs do not target NC. One possible scenario is that mutations in NC impair its chaperone activity during reverse transcription, leading to the formation of aberrant viral DNA ends that are not good substrates for INSTI binding. Point mutations in the CCHC motif of the NC zinc finger domains have been shown to severely impair viral infectivity, at least partly due to incomplete viral DNA processing and formation of aberrant viral DNA ends (30) (and confirmed here). In contrast, the NC mutations that arose in the presence of DTG (49) do not diminish particle infectivity or viral replication kinetics, and the integration efficiency of NC-G19S is higher than that of WT at early time points postinfection. These findings lead to the prediction that the NC mutations have a minimal effect on viral DNA ends. Using the NC-G19S mutant, we found that the sequences of 2-LTR circle junctions and virus-host junctions of integrated DNA are similar to those of WT. Together, these observations indicate that DTG-selected NC mutations do not modify the INSTI-intasome interaction through alteration of viral DNA ends. Our work also demonstrates that resistance mediated by the selected NC mutations is mechanistically distinct from that conferred by  \(3^{\prime}\)  PPT mutations, as the latter are characterized by integration-independent viral protein expression and a bypass of INSTI inhibition (39, 41, 42). In addition, the  \(3^{\prime}\)  PPT mutant tested here did not replicate in an HTLV-1 Tax-negative cell line (the SupT1 cell line), whereas the NC mutants selected in the presence of DTG replicated with kinetics similar to those of the WT.

As mentioned in Introduction, HIV-1 NC has been reported to have the ability to condense viral DNA and stimulate integration (18, 21-28). A consistent finding across different drug TOA formats is that the NC mutants selected in the presence of DTG reduce the time between completion of reverse transcription or uncoating and viral DNA integration. Because INSTIs act by binding the intasome—a complex of newly synthesized and  \(3^{\prime}\)  processed viral DNA ends and a multimer of IN (5, 7, 8)—reducing the time between viral DNA end formation and integration would effectively narrow the window of time available for INSTIs to bind the intasome and block integration.

HIV-1 preferentially integrates in SPADs—transcriptionally active, gene-dense regions of the host cell chromatin—and disfavors transcriptionally inactive regions of the chromatin, specifically LADs (64). In addition to showing more viral DNA integration at early time points relative to the WT, NC-G19S also shows a subtle but statistically significant shift in integration out of SPADs and into LADs. This shift is much less pronounced than that previously reported for CA mutants unable to interact with the host protein CPSF6 or in cells depleted for CPSF6 (65, 66, 70, 79). Given that 2-LTR circle formation and integration occur concurrently, NC mutations may alter NC binding to newly synthesized viral DNA, resulting in changes to postuncoating interaction between the intasome and host factors involved in the integration and host nonhomologous end joining pathway. We speculate that NC may have some role in integration site selection, or the faster kinetics of NC-G19S integration may cause an increase in integration into LADs, which tend to be localized to the nuclear periphery. Regardless of the mechanism, these results underscore the need for further investigation into the timing of uncoating, intasome formation, and interactions with host factors during infection and the role of NC in these events.

Several INSTI resistance mutations in IN have been reported in both in vitro and clinical settings (38, 80-82). Many of these IN mutations confer only a modest level of resistance to DTG (80). For instance, a major DTG resistance mutation, IN-R263K, reduces DTG susceptibility by  \(\sim 3\)  -fold (80). Notably, there is evidence that the emergence of mutants that exhibit only  \(\sim 4\)  -fold resistance to DTG increases the risk of VF (83). The level of resistance conferred by the NC mutations reported here is comparable to those conferred by these IN resistance mutations, suggesting that the presence of NC mutations could contribute to VF in PWH. In our previous study (49) and in this current work, we have shown that NC mutations emerge along with Env and IN mutations in a T cell line and in primary T cells. Previous work demonstrated that INSTI resistance mutations in IN often decrease viral fitness (77, 80, 84), but Env mutations rescue these defects (47-49). Notably, the NC mutations selected in the presence of DTG can increase the levels of INSTI resistance conferred by mutations in IN, indicating that NC mutations act in concert to reduce the susceptibility of HIV-1 to INSTIs.

In summary, this study provides insights into the role of NC in the HIV-1 replication cycle and underscores the importance of mutations outside drug-target genes in the development of INSTI resistance. This work, together with our previous studies, suggests that it may be necessary to analyze sequences outside IN for the cause of INSTI VF in PWH.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Cell lines and reagents

Human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells, TZM-bl cells (85), HeLa cells (American Type Culture Collection, CCL-2), and HeLa:mRuby-LaminB cells [a HeLa-derived cell line constitutively expressing an mRuby-LaminB fusion protein (71)] were maintained in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium supplemented with  \(10\%\)  fetal bovine serum (FBS) at  \(37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  in  \(5\%\) \(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\) . The SupT1 T cell line and SupT1huR5 T cell line (86) were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with  \(10\%\)  FBS at  \(37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  in  \(5\%\) \(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\) . The SupT1huR5 T cell line was a gift from J. Hoxie (Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA). DTG and BMS-378806 were purchased from MedChemExpress, and RPV and CAB were purchased from Cayman Chemical. The anti-HIV-1 Gag antibody (ab63917) was purchased from Abcam. LEN and anti-RT antibody (8C4) were obtained through the National Institutes of Health (NIH) HIV Reagent Program. Primary  \(\mathrm{CD4^{+}}\)  T cells were isolated from human PBMCs using an Easy-Sep Human  \(\mathrm{CD4^{+}}\)  T cell isolation kit (STEMCELL Technologies) according to the manufacturer's instructions. PBMCs were isolated using a ficoll gradient and stimulated with phytohemagglutinin (PHA-P;  \(2\mu \mathrm{g} / \mathrm{ml}\) ) for 3 to 5 days before infection and then cultured in interleukin-2 (IL-2;  \(50~\mathrm{U} / \mathrm{ml}\) ).

### Plasmids

The full-length HIV-1 molecular clones pNL4-3 (87), pCH185 (88), and pCH077 (89) were used in this study. A series of pNL4-3 NC mutants was described previously (49). pCH185 and pCH077 were gifts from C. Ochsenbauer and J. Kappes (University of Alabama at Birmingham). The pNL4-3/KFS clone, which does not express Env, was described previously (90). pNL4-3 IN-D116N was described previously (50). The NC regions with the indicated mutations were cloned into the pNL4-3/KFS using Spe I and Sbf I restriction sites. NC-H23C and H44C (30) were introduced into pNL4-3 and pNL4-3/KFS by

overlap PCR. The VSV-G-expressing plasmid, pHCMV-G, was a gift from J. Burns (91). The NL4-3-derived mScarlet reporter virus plasmid, pNL4-3 mScarlet.6ATRi KFS, and NL4-3 nanoLuc reporter virus plasmid, pNL4-3 nanoLuc.6ATRi KFS, were constructed on the basis of previously described pNL-LucR.6ATRi-BaL.ecto (51). The genetic information and the related DNA materials were gifts from C. Ochsenbauer (University of Alabama at Birmingham). The DNA fragments containing the modified encephalomyocarditis virus 6ATR internal ribosome entry site element (6ATRi) to replace the renilla luciferase with mScarlet-I3 or nanoLuc were synthesized by Twist Bioscience. The DNA fragments were cloned into pNL4-3/KFS using Hpa I and Xho I restriction sites. To increase the genetic stability of mScarlet-I3 and NanoLuc, CG dinucleotides in the reporter-coding genes were removed after the codon optimization (52). The HIV-1 helper construct pcHELP lacks both the packaging signal and primer-binding site and expresses all viral proteins except Nef and Env (92). pcHELP-GFPCA is a derivative of pcHELP in which GFP is inserted between the MA and CA domains of Gag, producing a GFP-CA fusion protein following proteolytic processing during viral maturation (20). The NC-G19S mutant derivatives were generated by inserting a gBlock (Integrated DNA Technologies) containing the G19S substitution in the Gag coding region, followed by subcloning into both pcHELP and pcHELP-GFPCA to yield pcHELP-G19S and pcHELP-GFPCA-NCG19S, respectively. The HIV-1-based vector pHmNG-  \(\Delta\) Gag contains an mNeonGreen (mNG) reporter gene in place of the nef gene and lacks Env expression. A frameshift mutation was introduced into gag by SphI digestion followed by removal of  \(3^{\prime}\)  overhang nucleotides using Klenow fragment, resulting in a premature stop codon.

### Preparation of virus stocks

HEK293T cells were transfected with HIV-1 proviral DNA using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer's instructions. VSV-G-pseudotyped viruses were prepared by cotransfecting HEK293T cells with pNL4-3/KFS and pHCMV-G at a DNA ratio of 10:1. At 48 hours posttransfection (26 hours for VSV-G-pseudotyped virus), virus-containing supernatants were filtered through a  \(0.45\mathrm{-}\mu \mathrm{m}\)  membrane filter (Merck Millipore). The amount of virus in the supernatant was quantified by RT assay as previously described (49). To generate GFP-CA-labeled virions containing the mNG reporter genome, 293T cells were cotransfected using polyethyleneimine (Polysciences) with the following plasmids: pCHELP-GFPCA and pCHELP (or their NC-G19S variants) at a 1:10 plasmid ratio (total of  \(3\mu \mathrm{g}\)  of DNA), pHmNG-  \(\Delta Gag\) \((7\mu \mathrm{g})\)  and pHCMV-G  \((2\mu \mathrm{g})\) . Approximately 24 hours posttransfection, virus-containing supernatants were collected, filtered, and concentrated by ultracentrifugation  \((100,000g\)  for 1.5 hours at  \(4^{\circ}C)\)  through a  \(20\%\)  w/v) sucrose cushion in  \(1\times\)  phosphate-buffered saline.

### Western blotting of viral proteins

Cell- and virus-associated proteins were solubilized in lysis buffer  \([30\mathrm{mMNaCl},50\mathrm{mM}\)  tris-HCl  \((\mathrm{pH}7.5)\) \(0.5\%\)  (v/v) Triton X-100,  \(10\mathrm{mM}\)  iodoacetamide, and complete PR inhibitor (Roche)]. Lysates boiled in  \(6\times\)  loading buffer  \([7\mathrm{ml}\)  of  \(0.5\mathrm{M}\)  tris-HCl,  \(0.4\%\)  w/v) SDS,  \(3.8\mathrm{g}\)  of glycerol,  \(1\mathrm{g}\)  of SDS,  \(0.93\mathrm{g}\)  of dithiothreitol, and  \(1.2\mathrm{mg}\)  of bromophenol blue] were subjected to SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride membranes Merck Millipore). After blocking with Azure Fluorescent Blot Blocking Buffer (Azure Biosystems), membranes were probed with indicated antibodies at  \(4^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  overnight and then incubated for 1 hour

with species-specific AzureSpectra Fluorescent Secondary Antibodies (Azure Biosystems). Bands were detected by fluorescence with a Sapphire Biomolecular Imager (Azure Biosystems) and quantified using ImageJ software.

### Quantification of viral RNA in the virion

Before viral RNA extraction, the virus supernatant from transfected 293T cells was treated with  \(20\mathrm{U}\)  of deoxyribonuclease I (DNase I; Thermo Fisher Scientific) at  \(37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  for 1 hour. Viral RNA was extracted with QIAamp Viral RNA Kits (QIAGEN). Viral RNA was detected by QuantStudio 3 Real-Time PCR systems and TaqMan Fast Virus 1-Step Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using the following primer/ probe set (93): forward primer GagF1  \((5^{\prime}\) -CTAGAACGATTCG-CAGTTAATCCT-  \(3^{\prime}\) ), reverse primer GagR1  \((5^{\prime}\) -CTATCCTTTGATGCACACAATAGAG-  \(3^{\prime}\) ), and probe P-HUS-103  \((5^{\prime}\) -FAMCATCAGAAGGCTGTAGACAAATACTGGGA-TAMRA-  \(3^{\prime}\) ). The cycling conditions were reverse transcription  \((50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}, 5\mathrm{min}\) , and  \(95^{\circ}\mathrm{C}, 20\mathrm{s})\)  and 40 cycles of denaturation  \((95^{\circ}\mathrm{C}, 3\mathrm{s})\)  and extension  \((60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}, 30\mathrm{s})\) .

### Viral infection and DNA isolation

Before infection, VSV-G-pseudotyped viruses were treated with  \(20\mathrm{U}\)  of DNase I at  \(37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  for 1 hour. A total of  \(5.0\times 10^{5}\)  SupT1 T cell lines were exposed to DNase I-treated, VSV-G-pseudotyped virus and placed at  \(4^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  for  \(30\mathrm{min}\)  for entry synchronization. Viral inputs were normalized by RT activity. Cells were incubated at  \(37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  for 3,6, 9, 12, and 24 hours postsynchronization. At indicated times, total DNA was extracted using the QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit (QIAGEN), and viral DNA was measured by qPCR. As a negative control, VSV-G-pseudotyped viruses were heat-inactivated at  \(95^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  for 1 hour.

### Sequence analysis of 2-LTR junction

Twenty-four hours postinfection with VSV-G-pseudotyped viruses, total DNA from the infected SupT1 T cell line was extracted as described above. The 2-LTR circle junction was amplified using PrimeSTAR GXL DNA polymerase (Takara Bio) with the following primers (93): forward primer SSF4  \((5^{\prime}\)  -TGGTTAGACCAGATCTGAGCCT-  \(3^{\prime}\)  ) and reverse primer LTR-R5  \((5^{\prime}\)  -AGGTAGCCTTGTGTGTGGTAGATCC-  \(3^{\prime}\)  ). The PCR amplicon was purified and cloned into pCR-Blunt II-TOPO vector (Thermo Fisher Scientific) per the manufacturer's instructions. The 2-LTR junction sequence was determined by Sanger sequencing (Poochon Scientific) using the M13 reverse primer.

### Integration site analysis

HIV-1 integration site analysis (ISA) was performed as previously described (94, 95). Briefly,  \(4\mu \mathrm{g}\)  of genomic DNA from each experimental condition was fragmented, A-tailed, and linker-ligated (NEBNext Ultra II FS, E7805L). Linker-mediated PCR targeted amplification and indexing of both  \(5^{\prime}\)  LTR and  \(3^{\prime}\)  LTR HIV-human integration junctions, and the prepared library was sequenced by Illumina MiSeq with paired end reads (Illumina MS-102-2002). Canonical ISA (complete LTR) and genome preference analysis were performed using a custom bioinformatic pipeline described in (95).

Aberrant ISA (noncanonical LTR junctions) was performed using an adapted bioinformatic pipeline (63). The FASTAQ files were prepared by being converted to their reverse complements using Seqtk (https://github.com/lh3/seqtk) to accommodate the input requirement of the previously described pipeline (63).  \(5^{\prime}\)  LTR and  \(3^{\prime}\)  LTR were analyzed

individually using the pipeline because they were sequenced separately, and the results for the same sample were integrated afterward. Primers for ISA are the following: 3LTR_PCR1  \((5^{\prime}\)  TGTGACTCTGGTAACTAGAGATCCCTC-  \(3^{\prime}\)  ), 5LTR_PCR1  \((5^{\prime}\)  TCAGGGAAGTAGCCTTGTGTGTGGT-  \(3^{\prime}\)  ), TLinkerMID_P1  \((5^{\prime}\)  - AGTTCAGACGTGTGCTCTTC-  \(3^{\prime}\)  ), 3LTR_PCR2  \((5^{\prime}\)  - AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACACAGGCGAAGACACTCTTCCCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCTNNNNNNTCATCGAGCCTTTTAGTCAGTGTGGAAAATC-  \(3^{\prime}\)  ), 5LTR_PCR2  \((5^{\prime}\)  -AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACACATAGAGGCACACTCTTCCCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCTNNNNNNTACTATATGTCTTCTTTGGGACCAAATTAGCC-  \(3^{\prime}\)  ), and Linker_  \(P2^{*}\) \((5^{\prime}\)  CAAGCAGAAGACGGCATACGAGATXXXXXXGTGACTGGAGTTCAGACGTGTGCTCTTCCGATC-  \(3^{\prime}\)  ).\*\*\*\*\*\*\* is 8-nt index for (de)multiplex of individual samples.

### Live-cell imaging

Live-cell imaging of HIV-1 uncoating was performed as previously described (20). Briefly, HeLa:mRuby-LaminB cells were seeded at  \(4\times 10^{4}\)  cells per well in ibiTreated  \(\mu\)  -slides (Ibidi) 1 day before infection. Cells were challenged with GFP-CA-labeled viruses at a low MOI (~2 nuclear particles per cell) with polybrene  \((10~\mu \mathrm{g / ml})\)  Sigma-Aldrich) via spinoculation (1200g for 1 hour at  \(15^{\circ}\mathrm{C})\)  allowing virus binding without internalization (96). Following spinoculation, the medium was replaced with prewarmed media to initiate viral internalization (defined as time 0). Aphidicolin  \((10~\mu \mathrm{g / ml})\)  was added at the time of infection to inhibit cell division. Live-cell imaging was performed using a Nikon Eclipse Ti-E microscope equipped with a Yokogawa CSU-W1 spinning disk confocal unit, PlanApochromat  \(100\times\)  numerical aperture 1.49 oil immersion objective, and  \(488\mathrm{-nm}\)  (GFP) and  \(561\mathrm{-nm}\)  (mRuby) lasers. Images were acquired using a  \(561\mathrm{-nm}\)  long pass dichroic mirror and two ORCAfusion BT cameras (Hamamatsu). A Tokai Hit stage-top incubator was used to maintain cells at  \(37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  Time-lapse z-stacks (12 slices at  \(0.4\mathrm{-}\mu \mathrm{m}\)  intervals) were collected every  \(20\mathrm{min}\)  starting approximately 4 hours postinfection and continued for 18 hours. Nuclear GFPCA spots were manually tracked using Nikon Elements, and their disappearance times were recorded.

### Quantification of viral cDNA in the infected cells

Viral and cellular DNA was quantified by qPCR using QuantStudio 3 Real-Time PCR systems and TaqMan Advanced Fast qPCR mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with the following primer/probe sets (93, 97): late RT products  \((\mathrm{U}5\Psi)\)  forward primer HIV LTR_GagF  \(5^{\prime}\) -GAGATCCCTCAGACCCTTTTAGT-  \(3^{\prime}\) , reverse primer HIV LTR_GagR  \(5^{\prime}\) -TTCAGCAAGCCGAGTCCT-  \(3^{\prime}\) , and probe P-HUSSS1  \((5^{\prime}\) -FAM-TAGTGTGTGCCGTCTGTTGTGTGAC-TAMRA-  \(3^{\prime}\) ); 2-LTR circle: forward primer SSF4  \((5^{\prime}\) -TGGTTAGACCAGATCTGAGCCT-  \(3^{\prime}\) ), reverse primer LTR-R5  \((5^{\prime}\) -AGGTAGCCTTGTGTGTGGTAGATCC-  \(3^{\prime}\) ), and probe P-HUS-SS1. Host CCR5 was detected using forward primer CCR5-For  \((5^{\prime}\) -CCAGAAGAGCTGAGACATCCG-  \(3^{\prime}\) ), reverse primer CCR5-Rev  \((5^{\prime}\) -GCCAAGCAGCTGAGAGGTTACT-  \(3^{\prime}\) ), and probe P-CCR5-01  \((5^{\prime}\) -FAM-TCCCCTACAAGAAACTCTCCCCGG-TAMRA-  \(3^{\prime}\) ). The cycling conditions were as follows: initial denaturation  \((95^{\circ}\mathrm{C}, 20\mathrm{s})\)  and 40 cycles of denaturation  \((95^{\circ}\mathrm{C}, 1\mathrm{s})\)  and extension  \((60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}, 20\mathrm{s})\) . Standard curves for late RT product, 2-LTR circle, and CCR5 were based on pNL4-3, pJB1041 (30), and pRB2569 (93), respectively. To detect integrated DNA, the nested Alu-LTR PCR method was applied as previously

described (97). The first PCR was performed using PrimeSTAR GXL DNA polymerase (Takara Bio) with Alu-HIV  \((5^{\prime}\)  -TCCCAGCTACTCGGGAGGCTGAGG-  \(3^{\prime}\)  ) and M661  \((5^{\prime}\)  -CCTGCGTCGAGAGATCTCCTCTG-  \(3^{\prime}\)  ) primers. The first PCR cycling conditions were as follows: initial denaturation  \((98^{\circ}\mathrm{C},10\mathrm{s})\)  ,22 cycles of denaturation  \((98^{\circ}\mathrm{C},10\mathrm{s})\)  , annealing  \((60^{\circ}\mathrm{C},15\mathrm{s})\)  ,and extension  \((68^{\circ}\mathrm{C},10\mathrm{min})\)  The first PCR product was diluted 10-fold and used as a template for measuring R/U5 DNA using M667 primer  \((5^{\prime}\)  -GGCTAACTAGGGAACCCACTGC-  \(3^{\prime}\)  ),AA55 primer  \((5^{\prime}\)  -CTGCTAGAGATTTTCCACACTGAC-  \(3^{\prime}\)  ), and HIV-FAM probe  \((5^{\prime}\)  -FAMTAGTGTGTGCCCGTCTGTTGTGTGAC-TAMRA-  \(3^{\prime}\)

### Single-round infectivity assay

Single-round infectivity assays were performed as previously described (49). TZM-bl cells  \((1.0\times 10^{4}\)  cells) in 96-well plates were incubated with RT-normalized virus stocks. At the indicated time postinfection, luciferase activity was measured using the Britelite plus reporter gene assay system (PerkinElmer) and the GloMax Navigator microplate luminometer (Promega). SupT1 or PHA-stimulated primary  \(\mathrm{CD4^+}\)  T cells  \((2.0\times 10^{6}\)  cells) were incubated with the RT-normalized VSV-G-pseudotyped nanoLuc reporter virus at  \(37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  for 2 hours. Following incubation, the cells were washed and plated in 96-well flat-bottom plates and incubated at  \(37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  in the presence of various concentrations of DTG. Nano luciferase activity was measured using the Nano-Glo luciferase system (Promega) according to the manufacturer's instructions.

### Virus replication kinetic assays

Virus replication was monitored in the SupT1 T cell line as previously described (49). Briefly, SupT1 cells were incubated with the indicated pNL4-3 clones  \((1.0\mu \mathrm{g}\)  of DNA/  \(1.0\times 10^{6}\)  cells) in the presence of DEAE-dextran  \((700~\mu \mathrm{g / ml})\)  at  \(37^{\circ}C\)  for  \(15\mathrm{min}\) . Transfected cells  \((1.5\times 10^{5}\)  cells) were plated in 96-well flat-bottom plates and incubated at  \(37^{\circ}C\)  in the presence of a range of concentrations of DTG (0 to  \(300\mathrm{nM}\) ). Aliquots of supernatants were collected to measure RT activity, and cells were split 1:3 every other day with fresh drug and medium.  \(\mathrm{IC}_{50}\)  values were calculated on the basis of the AUC of the replication kinetics.  \(\mathrm{IC}_{50}\)  was defined as the amount of inhibitor required to reduce the AUC by  \(50\%\) .

### TOA assay

TZM-bl cells  \((1.0\times 10^{4}\)  cells) in 96-well plates were incubated with NL4-3 variants. SupT1  \((5.0\times 10^{5}\)  cells) or HeLa  \((4.0\times 10^{4}\)  cells) in 48-well plates were incubated with VSV-G-pseudotyped NL4-3 mScarlet reporter virus at  \(4^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  for  \(30\mathrm{min}\)  for entry synchronization, followed by incubation at  \(37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) . The viral input was normalized by RT activity. At the indicated time postinfection,  \(3\mu \mathrm{M}\)  BMS-378806 (for NL4-3 virus),  \(1\mu \mathrm{M}\)  RPV,  \(100\mathrm{nM}\)  LEN, or  \(1\mu \mathrm{M}\)  DTG was added. Luciferase activity was measured at 48 hours postinfection using the Britelite plus reporter gene assay system (PerkinElmer) and the GloMax Navigator microplate luminometer (Promega). mScarlet expression was measured at 48 hours postinfection with an LSR-Fortessa (BD Biosciences) and analyzed by FlowJo software (Tree Star Inc.).

### Long-term propagation of HIV-1 in PBMCs in the presence of DTG

Selection of HIV-1 variants resistant to DTG was performed by serial passaging of the HIV-1-infected PBMCs with increasing concentrations of DTG. Freshly thawed PBMCs were activated weekly

with IL-2 (50 U/ml) and PHA-P (2  \(\mu\) g/ml). At 6 to 7 days postinfection, the infected cells were split, and cultures were replenished with fresh drug and PBMCs. To monitor viral replication in the presence of DTG, a small portion of the infected cell culture was cocultured with the SupT1huR5 T cell line in a separate culture without DTG on day 5. Dose escalation was performed when cytopathic effects in the SupT1huR5 T cell line were observed within a 2-day coculture period. At the indicated time points, genomic DNA was extracted from infected cells using the DNeasy Blood and Tissue Minikit (QIAGEN), and the Gag-Pol and Env-Nef coding regions were amplified by PrimeSTAR GXL DNA polymerase (Takara Bio) and sequenced by Sanger or Oxford Nanopore methods (Psomagen) using previously described primers (98, 99).

**Study Objectives**
The objective of this project is to systematically extract and curate data related to HIV drug resistance from published reports. For each paper, identify and summarize information on:

1. HIV nucleotide or amino-acid sequences obtained from clinical samples, including GenBank accession numbers.
2. The populations from whom HIV sequences were obtained.
3. The clinical samples and sequencing methods used.
4. Antiretroviral \(ARV\) treatment histories of the individuals whose samples were sequenced.

**Question 1 – Does the paper report HIV sequences from patient samples?**
**Goal:** Determine whether the study generated new HIV nucleotide or amino-acid sequences, or reported lists of mutations, directly from clinical samples obtained from individuals with HIV \(ART-naïve or ART-experienced\).
**Answer “Yes” if the paper:**

- States that genetic sequencing, genotypic resistance testing, Sanger sequencing, next-generation sequencing, or single-genome sequencing was performed on clinical samples such as plasma, serum, PBMCs, proviral DNA, or dried blood spots.
- Indicates that sequencing was done on samples from patients, participants, subjects, blood donors, newly diagnosed or newly infected individuals, PLWH/PWH, or cohorts of individuals with HIV.
- States that surveillance for transmitted or acquired drug resistance was performed and generated new sequence data.
- Reports GenBank accession numbers for sequences generated in the study.

**Answer “No” if:**

- Only laboratory strains \(e.g., HXB2, IIIB, NL4-3, BAL, LAI\) or site-directed mutants were studied.
- The paper is a review or meta-analysis using sequences reported in other studies or downloaded from databases without generating new sequences.

**Question 2 – Does the paper report in vitro drug susceptibility data?**
**Goal:** Determine whether the paper quantifies HIV in vitro susceptibility to ARV drugs.
**Answer “Yes” if the paper:**

- States that phenotypic susceptibility testing, phenotypic resistance testing, or a drug susceptibility assay was performed.
- Reports IC₅₀, EC₅₀, EC₉₀, fold change in susceptibility, or similar measures.
- Describes a susceptibility assay \(e.g., PhenoSense/Monogram, Antivirogram/Virco\) or gives details on cells, drug titrations, and reporter readouts.
- Specifies the virus used for testing \(e.g., clinical isolate, site-directed mutant, virus from in vitro passage\).

Otherwise, answer “No”.

**Question 3 – Were sequences from the paper made publicly available?**
**Goal:** Determine whether newly generated HIV sequences or raw reads were deposited in public repositories \(e.g., GenBank, SRA, DDBJ, ENA\).
**Answer “Yes” if the paper:**

- Provides GenBank accession numbers \(typically two letters followed by digits\) in the Methods, Results, a Supplementary Table, or Data Availability statement.
- States that sequences have been submitted to GenBank or another public database, even if accession numbers are “pending.”
- States that raw reads are available in SRA or other sequence-read repositories.

**Answer “No” if:**

# Emergence of in-vitro resistance to lenacapavir is similar across HIV-1 subtypes

Objective: To assess the potential in-vitro emergence of resistance mutations to the capsid inhibitor lenacapavir (LEN) in clinical samples from subtype B versus non-B HIV-1 subtype.

Design: Twenty-four clinical isolates with non-B or B HIV-1 subtype were assessed for their in vitro susceptibility to LEN and their potential to develop resistance to LEN in viral breakthrough experiments.

Methods: The HIV-1 gag-protease DNA fragment from various HIV-1 isolates was cloned (pXXLAI vector), and viruses were generated by transfection. Viruses were tested for antiretroviral drug susceptibility, and subjected to selection with LEN in tissue culture for up to 46 days. The capsid and reverse transcriptase sequence from the selected viruses were analyzed to determine the presence of resistance mutations.

Results: Samples with HIV-1 subtype A1, AE, AG, B, C, D, F1, G, and H were evaluated. Wild-type susceptibility to LEN  \((\mathrm{EC}_{50}21 - 115~\mathrm{pM})\)  was observed across all subtypes tested. Resistance selections in non-B subtypes led to the emergence of the same mutations with similar timeframe as in subtype B. The most prevalent capsid mutations selected across all subtypes were N74D (9 of 25 cultures), Q67H (4/25), and T107N (4/25), while M66I, K70R/S, and N74H were also observed.

Conclusion: In-vitro susceptibility to LEN was not affected by the subtype of the samples tested, and selected resistance mutations were not significantly different across HIV-1 subtypes. These data indicate that LEN is a pan-genotypic inhibitor of HIV-1 that can be effective in all geographical settings, regardless of HIV-1 subtypes.


Keywords: capsid, HIV-1, lenacapavir, N74D, subtype

## Materials and methods

### Reagents

LEN, dolutegravir (DTG), darunavir (DRV), tenofovir alafenamide (TAF), and efavirenz (EFV) were synthesized at Gilead Sciences (Foster City, California, USA). HEK293T cells (293T cells) used for virus production were purchased from American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, Virginia, USA). MT-2 cells were obtained from the National Institutes of Health AIDS Research and Reference Reagent Program (Germantown, Maryland, USA). The viral plasmid pXXLAI used to generate the viruses was a gift from John Mellors. The plasmid was derived from the infectious clone pLAI3.2 which was modified to contain an XmaI and an XbaI

restriction site within the HIV reverse transcriptase (RT) gene [12] to facilitate cloning. To clone the HIV-1 gagpro fragment, the natural SfoI and engineered XmaI restriction sites were used (see below). GlutaMAX RPMI 1640 culture medium, Gibco DMEM high glucose, penicillin  \((10000\mathrm{U / ml})\)  , streptomycin  \((10000\mu \mathrm{g / ml})\)  and  \(100\mathrm{X}\)  HEPES were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific (Waltham, Massachusetts, USA). Fetal bovine serum (FBS) was purchased from HyClone Laboratories (Logan, Utah, USA). Cell culture media were supplemented with  \(10\%\)  heat-inactivated FBS,  \(5\mathrm{ml}\)  of penicillin  \((10000\mathrm{U / ml})\)  and Streptomycin  \((10000\mu \mathrm{g / ml})\)  and  \(5\mathrm{ml}\)  of  \(100\mathrm{X}\)  HEPES per  \(500\mathrm{ml}\)  of medium.

### Clinical samples

Patient plasma samples were obtained from studies GS-US-380-1490, GS-US-292-0104, GS-US-200-4334, and GS-US-200-4625. Patient informed consent was obtained prior to the collection of the clinical samples used in this study. The plasma samples were from participants who were treatment naive to the capsid inhibitor class, had diverse HIV-1 subtypes (A, A1, AE, AG, B, C, D, F1, G, H), and had HIV-1 RNA ranging from 3130 to 647000 copies/ml. HIV-1 subtype determination was based on the baseline protease/reverse transcriptase sequence of the participants that was analyzed prior to enrollment in the respective studies.

### Subtype characterization

Subtype determination from capsid sequences was conducted using the Rega Subtyping Tool 3.0 (https://www.genomedetective.com/app/typingtool/hiv/) as well as a proprietary method based on BLAST analyses against a curated HIV reference sequence library. For less confident subtype calls (<95% sequence identity) from BLAST analyses, phylogenetic and recombination analyses were performed. Maximum likelihood phylogenetic trees were generated using FastTree v2.1.11 employing the Jukes Cantor model with 1000 bootstraps.

### Sample cloning

HIV-1 RNA was extracted from  \(50\mu \mathrm{l}\)  of plasma using the Mag Max-96Viral RNA isolation kit (Thermo Fisher, Waltham, Massachusetts, USA, # AMB 18365) following manufacturer's instructions, and eluted in  \(90\mu \mathrm{l}\)  of buffer. The HIV-1 RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA and amplified using the single-step Superscript IV One-Step RT PCR System (Thermo Fisher, # 12594100). HIV-1 DNA amplification was generated through two rounds of PCR (first round PCR primers: U563 [GCTTAAGCCTCAATAAAGCTTGCCTTG; HXB2 nucleotide (nt) 516 to 542] and RT155 [GGCCCAATTTTGAAATTTCCCTTCC; reverse complement of HXB2 nt 2678 to 2704]; second round PCR primers: U613-IF [ATCTC-TAGCAGTGGCGCCCGAACAGGGACTTGAAAG; HXB2 nt 625 to 660] and RC-5-HIV-Xma-IF [GGCCATCCATCCCGGGCTTTAATTTTACTGGTACAGTTTC; reverse complement of HXB2 nt 2565 to

2604]. Reactions were conducted in a  \(50\mu \mathrm{l}\)  volume containing  \(10\mu \mathrm{l}\)  of RNA,  \(25\mu \mathrm{l}\)  2X Platinum Super Fi II PCR master mix (Thermo Fisher, #12368010),  \(2.5\mu \mathrm{l}\)  of  \(10\mu \mathrm{mol} / 1\)  primers each,  \(0.5\mu \mathrm{l}\)  of superscript IV RT, and  \(9.5\mu \mathrm{l}\)  of water. The HIV-1 gag-protease fragment from these plasma samples was amplified by two rounds of 30 cycles of PCR and subcloned into Zero Blunt TOPO pCR vector (Thermo Fisher, #450031). The obtained vector was used to transform one shot TOP10 chemically competent cells (Thermo Fisher, #C404003), and colonies of interest were grown overnight. The plasmid DNA was prepared (Qiagen, #27104), followed by restriction enzyme digest with SfoI and XmaI and ligation with T4 DNA ligase (New England Biolabs, #M0467S) into wildtype pXXLAI linearized with the same enzymes. The ligated vector was used to transform stable competent cells (New England Biolabs, #C3040H). The transformed bacteria were grown overnight, and the plasmid DNA was purified and sequenced at ELIM Biopharmaceuticals (Hayward, California, USA). Sequence analysis was conducted using Geneious Prime software version 2024.0.5 (Aukland, New Zealand).

### Virus production

pXXLAI DNA plasmids were transfected into HEK293T cells using the transfection reagent Lipofectamine 3000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, # L3000015) using  \(7\mu \mathrm{g}\)  of the viral plasmid DNA in 2 million 293T cells seeded in T-25 cell culture flasks in a 6-ml volume 1 day before transfection. Cultures were replenished with fresh media  \(24\mathrm{h}\)  after transfection. The cell culture supernatant containing the virus stock was harvested at 48 and  \(72\mathrm{h}\)  after transfection, characterized by p24 ELISA, and tested in infectivity assays.

### Multicycle phenotypic assay

Drug susceptibility of the HIV-1 isolates was determined in a 5-day multicycle antiviral assay in MT-2 cells using a luciferase-based viability readout (CellTiterGlo; Promega, Madison, Wisconsin, USA) [13]. Briefly, MT-2 cells (2.4 million) were incubated with virus for  \(2.5\mathrm{h}\)  at  \(37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) . The amount of virus used was normalized to yield a signal-to-noise  \((S / N)\)  ratio in the range of 4-7, which was equivalent to an MOI around 0.003 for wild-type HIV \(1_{\mathrm{HIB}}\)  based on the provided titer. The S/N ratio was calculated from the  \(300\mathrm{nmol / l}\)  DTG control (maximum cell survival) and the no-drug control (minimum cell survival). Five-fold dilutions of the drugs of interest were transferred in triplicate to 96-well plates. Maximum concentration tested were  \(0.01\mu \mathrm{mol} / \mathrm{l}\)  for LEN,  \(1\mu \mathrm{mol} / \mathrm{l}\)  for TAF,  \(0.1\mu \mathrm{mol} / \mathrm{l}\)  for EFV,  \(0.5\mu \mathrm{mol} / \mathrm{l}\)  for DRV, and  \(0.15\mu \mathrm{mol} / \mathrm{l}\)  for DTG. After incubation, the infected MT-2 cells were diluted 1:14 to a concentration of 0.17 million cells/mL with tissue culture medium, and  \(50~\mu \mathrm{l}\)  of cell suspension was transferred to all wells in the plates. After 5 days of incubation at  \(37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  ( \(5\%\) \(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\) ,  \(95\%\)  humidity),  \(100~\mu \mathrm{l}\)  of CellTiterGlo reagent was added to each well and luminescence was measured (Envision plate reader, Envision, USA).

reader; PerkinElmer, Shelton, Connecticut, USA). Percentage inhibition in the drug wells in comparison to the DTG control, and the effective concentration to inhibit  \(50\%\)  of viral replication  \(\mathrm{(EC_{50})}\)  were plotted and calculated using Excel (Microsoft, Redmond, Washington, USA) and XL Fit (IDBS, Alameda, California, USA). Statistical significance of the  \(\mathrm{EC}_{50}\)  fold-changes was calculated using Excel (two-tailed Student's t-test; with  \(P < 0.05\)  considered significant).

### Breakthrough resistance selection

Methods to conduct breakthrough infections and breakthrough resistance selection were previously published [14,15]. Briefly, MT-2 cells (2.4 million) were incubated with virus (same volume as above) for  \(2.5\mathrm{h}\)  at  \(37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  in 1-ml volume. After the infection, the cells were resuspended in RPMI medium at a concentration of 10 000 infected cells/100  \(\mu\) l of RPMI/well and seeded in triplicate along with an infected no-drug control. The plates were incubated for  \(24\mathrm{h}\)  at  \(37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)  with  \(5\%\) \(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\) . LEN and lamivudine (3TC) were tested at concentrations of  \(0.5\mathrm{x}, 1\mathrm{x}, 2\mathrm{x}, 4\mathrm{x}, 8\mathrm{x},\)  and  \(16\mathrm{x}\)  their MT-2  \(\mathrm{EC}_{95}\)  value of 0.23 and  \(20\mu \mathrm{mol} / \mathrm{l}\) , respectively. The concentrations for LEN were 0.06, 0.23, 0.46, 0.92, 1.84, and  \(3.68\mathrm{nmol} / \mathrm{l}\) , and for 3TC 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, and  \(320\mu \mathrm{mol} / \mathrm{l}\) . The diluted drugs were added  \(24\mathrm{h}\)  after plating the infected cells. Viral breakthrough was assessed over a period of 46 days, during which cell cultures were maintained by routine passaging (1:3 for LEN and 1:10 for 3TC, adjusted based on viral growth difference between the two conditions) every 4-5 days and adding uninfected MT-2 cells (10000 cells/85  \(\mu\) l/well), and  \(100\mu \mathrm{l}\)  of diluted drug in RPMI media. At each time point during the assay (Day 4, 10, 14, 19, 24, 28, 32, 37, 41, and 46 postinfection), wells were visually inspected on a light microscope for the development of virus-induced cytopathic effect (CPE). Viral supernatants were harvested  \((100\mu \mathrm{l})\)  and stored at  \(-80^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) . Cultures showing evidence of CPE were analyzed for genotypic changes at Elim Biopharmaceuticals (Hayward, California, USA).

## Results

Clinical samples with diverse HIV-1 subtypes were used to evaluate the susceptibility to LEN across these subtypes, and resistance selection with LEN in samples with various HIV-1 subtypes were conducted.

### Sample cloning and drug susceptibility

The gag-protease DNA fragment from a total of 24 patient samples was cloned into pXXLAI, including 15 samples with non-B HIV-1 subtype (HIV-1 subtypes A1=1, AE=2, AG=3, C=1, D=3, F1=2, G=2, H=1) and nine with HIV-1 B subtype. The initial determination of sample subtype based on pol sequencing was confirmed for 22 of the 24 samples based on capsid sequences using

the Rega Subtyping Tool 3.0 or a proprietary BLAST method. The two discrepant samples initially characterized as subtype D and H (based on pol sequence) were both found to have subtype A1 in the Rega/BLAST analyses of the CA sequence. These minor differences may have stemmed from the shorter length of capsid sequences compared to pol sequences.

Drug susceptibilities of the 24 clinical isolates were characterized in the MT-2 multicycle phenotypic assay. The overall mean LEN  \(\mathrm{EC}_{50}\)  for all viral isolates was  \(0.067\mathrm{nmol} / 1\)  (standard deviation [SD]: 0.027) (Fig. 1). The average fold change in susceptibility to LEN in all tested non-B HIV-1 subtype isolates was 1.0-fold (ranging from 0.3 to 1.8) compared with wild-type control, and was 1.1-fold (ranging from 0.6 to 1.6) in B HIV-1 subtype isolates. These data indicate that LEN has a similar picomolar potency across all HIV-1 subtypes tested. The mean  \(\mathrm{EC}_{50}\)  of control drugs DTG, DRV, TAF, and EFV (representative drugs from the four main classes of antiretroviral drugs: integrase strand-transfer inhibitor, protease inhibitor, nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor, nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor [NNRTI], respectively), were  \(3.2\mathrm{nmol} / 1\)  (SD: 2.0),  \(6.0\mathrm{nmol} / 1\)  (SD: 3.8),  \(8.3\mathrm{nmol} / 1\)  (SD: 4.8) and  \(3.7\mathrm{nmol} / 1\)  (SD: 2.3), respectively, all within the expected range of  \(\mathrm{EC}_{50}\)  measurements.

### Breakthrough resistance selection

Resistance selections using fixed concentrations of drugs were performed with LEN and 3TC (control drug) in MT-2 cells infected with patient isolates or pXXLAI control  \((N = 25)\) . Viral breakthrough in the LEN cultures

was observed at low LEN concentrations (0.5X-2X  \(\mathrm{EC}_{95}\) ) as evidenced by CPE at these concentrations (Fig. 2, Fig. 3). CPE was not observed at higher LEN concentrations of 8X and 16X  \(\mathrm{EC}_{95}\) , and were rarely observed at 4X  \(\mathrm{EC}_{95}\)  (only in two of 25 cultures), similar to prior observations [6]. In contrast, CPE associated with viral breakthrough was present at all concentrations tested (0.5X to 16X  \(\mathrm{EC}_{95}\) ) for the control drug 3TC (Fig. 2, Fig. 3), illustrating the emergence of 3TC molecular resistance.

### Resistance emergence and genotypic analyses

Population sequencing of the target proteins for LEN (CA) and 3TC (RT) was performed on the viral supernatants obtained at multiple stages of the breakthrough resistance selection. Mutations were first detected between Day 19 and Day 38. Emergence of similar LEN resistance-associated mutations (RAMs) was observed in both non-B and B HIV-1 subtypes. LEN RAMs were observed in 11 of 15 non-B subtypes isolates, including M66I/L, Q67H, K70R/S, N74D/H, A105I, and/or T107N/S in CA, and in five of 10 B subtype isolates (four isolates + pXXLAI control strain), including M66I, Q67H, N74D, and/or T107N/S in CA. The most prevalent emergent LEN RAM was N74D, which was observed in nine cultures across all subtypes. Other LEN mutations included Q67H (four cultures), T107N/S (T107N in four cultures, T107S in two cultures), K70R/S (three cultures), M66I/L (three cultures), and A105I (one culture). ## Discussion

We have generated a panel of HIV-1 recombinant patient isolates with diverse HIV-1 subtypes in order to expand data on the antiviral activity of LEN across multiple HIV-1 clades, and to evaluate, for the first time, the potential in-vitro emergence of mutations conferring resistance to LEN across these patient-derived viral isolates. Owing to its lack of proof-reading exonuclease activity, the HIV-1 reverse transcriptase enzyme that replicates the HIV genome is error-prone, with an estimated error rate of 1 change per 1700 base pairs replicated [16]. As a result, HIV-1 has acquired a great deal of variation and HIV-1 lineages have been organized in groups of sequences, so-called subtypes or clades, that share common ancestry [7,17,18]. In the United States and Europe, HIV-1 subtype B is the most common and has been studied extensively. A recent search of the Los Alamos National Laboratory HIV database indicated that  \(54\%\)  of full genome sequences (out of a total of 21 526 sequences) [19] had HIV-1 subtype B, although subtype B was estimated to represent only  \(8.5\%\)  of the current infected population [10], reflecting an imbalance of the available HIV-1 sequence data in comparison to the overall geographical burden of HIV-1 infection. In addition, studies of the HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein, which sequence can vary by about  \(20\%\)  across Group M subtypes [20], have shown that the evolution of the envelope under selective pressure differed depending on the HIV-1 subtype under study [21]. Similar observations have been made for some NNRTI mutations, where the V106M was found preferentially in HIV-1 subtype C compared to V106A in other subtypes [22]. As a result, it is key that studies such as ours be conducted in samples and populations that are

representative of the overall HIV-1 population in order to understand the potential effect of worldwide sequence diversity.

Interestingly, in contrast to the envelope protein, the sequence of the capsid protein is much less diverse, with about  \(95\%\)  sequence conservation across samples with diverse HIV-1 subtype in our dataset [20,23]. This high degree of homology is likely a reflection of the constraints associated with the need to maintain the relatively fixed CA structure in order to preserve its function. A mutagenesis analysis study indicated that CA was very sensitive to minor changes in the sequence, with mutant viruses often afflicted with high loss of replication capacity [24], suggesting that alterations of the CA sequence was very often associated with a high cost to the virus. This overall indicates that the CA protein may have little room for escape when subjected to immune pressure or when in contact with small molecule inhibitors. In our analysis of non-B subtype sequences under selective pressure with LEN, we have found that amino acid residues with emerging mutations were identical to the emerging mutations observed in B subtype, again suggesting that only a few changes in the LEN binding pocket may be structurally possible to escape the drug pressure, regardless of the HIV-1 subtype of the samples. This conclusion is also supported by a recent publication describing eight cases of people living with HIV-2 [25], who experienced virologic failure while receiving LEN: 4 of 8 had emergence of N73D in capsid (equivalent to N74D in HIV-1) and 1 of 8 had emergence of  \(\mathrm{Q66H + R69K}\)  in capsid (equivalent to  \(\mathrm{Q67H + K70R}\)  in HIV-1), showing a similar mutation outcome in HIV-2 and HIV-1. The emergence of N73D in a person with HIV-2 was also reported independently [26]. Overall, our dataset showed that only one change in one subtype D sample (virus #19, Fig. 2) was not previously described (M66L), and may have been more fit under the selection conditions, as the M66L site-directed mutant only conferred near four-fold reduced susceptibility to LEN (data not shown). Interestingly, the M66L and N74D mutations were found in separate replicates of the same culture (Fig. 2, Fig. 3), suggesting a similar effect of the mutations at the LEN concentration in those conditions.

Finally, we noted that the pattern of HIV-1 inhibition and emergence of resistance differed between LEN and the control drug 3TC. For LEN, viral growth and resistance emergence was rarely observed above  \(4\mathrm{XEC}_{95}\) , whereas with 3TC, viral growth was observed through to the highest dose tested  \((16\mathrm{XEC}_{95})\)  in most cultures. This may stem from the fact that the nucleoside drug 3TC needs to be phosphorylated to 3TC-triphosphate by cellular enzymes in order to be an active substrate for RT [27], whereas LEN does not need modification and is active immediately in cell culture. This difference could have led to a timing difference between the two drugs, giving an advantage to LEN. Another factor at play in these observations is that selection of resistance is a stochastic event that can vary based on the experimental conditions, such that replicate samples do not necessarily give rise to the exact same mutation pattern due to chance, as indicated above for sample #19 that showed different mutations in replicates. We acknowledge that the reduced number of replicates for some non-B subtypes was a limitation in our study, however, the resistance patterns observed in this limited dataset are consistent with prior data that defined the mutations associated with LEN resistance in vitro[1] and in vivo[28]. A separate dataset using a similar approach as ours was very recently disclosed at a conference [29] and showed a similar set of emerging mutations across various HIV-1 subtypes as we found in this report, reinforcing our finding that HIV-1 subtype is not a factor of influence for the development of LEN resistance. This finding is important, as LEN is poised to be used in diverse populations across the world particularly within the context of HIV prevention, and the data presented here support the use of LEN in people with diverse HIV-1 genetic lineages.

PAPER FULL TEXT # Detection of HIV-1 drug resistance in RNA and proviral DNA genotyping is variable both longitudinally and during repeat testing\* ## ABSTRACT Background: HIV-1 variants harboring resistance-associated mutations (RAMs) can be archived in viral reservoirs and then re-emerge. Given the dynamic properties of the latent reservoir and detection limits of genotypic assays, RAM persistence over time is incompletely understood. Objective: This retrospective analysis investigated RAM detection in adults with HIV. Study design: Genotyping of protease, reverse transcriptase, and integrase from 3 bictegravir/emtricitabine/ tenofovir alafenamide switch studies was included. Longitudinal analyses were performed for participants with combinations of RNA and proviral DNA genotype reports from \(\geq 2\) pre-switch timepoints. Reported RAMs assessed at 2 timepoints were categorized as \(100\%\) or \(50\%\) detection, and those assessed at \(\geq 3\) timepoints as persistent, lost, gained, or inconsistent detection. From each whole blood sample, reproducibility (\%) of proviral RAM reporting was the number of times the mutation was detected per number of assays run (2-4 replicates). Results: In 223 participants, of 262 RAMs tracked longitudinally over 2 timepoints, \(39\%\) (103/262) had \(100\%\) detection and \(61\%\) (159/262) had \(50\%\) detection, with \(64\%\) (101/159) detected at timepoint 2. In 25 participants with \(\geq 3\) timepoints, detection of 57 RAMs was categorized as persistent (19%; 11/57), lost (12%; 7/57), gained (26%; 15/57), or inconsistent (42%; 24/57). Mean (standard deviation) reproducibility of proviral RAM detection at 1 timepoint was \(80.9\%\) (27.2%) (336 RAMs from 70 participants). Conclusions: No consistent pattern of longitudinal RAM detection was observed. Reproducibility of proviral genotyping was high but variable. Since RAMs were not always consistently detected, an individual's cumulative resistance history should be considered for optimal treatment management. # 2. Study design ## 2.1. Study participants The study included treatment-experienced PWH aged \(\geq 18\) years, randomized to B/F/TAF or comparator regimens in studies GS-US-380-4449 (NCT03405935 [5,6]; \(\geq 65\) years), GS-US-380-4030 (NCT03110380 [7]), and GS-US-380-4580 (NCT03631732 [8]), with virologic suppression (HIV-1 RNA \(< 50\) copies/mL) for \(\geq 3 - 6\) months and no prior virologic failure on integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI)-containing regimens (GS-US-380-4030, GS-US-380-4580) or no HIV-1 RNA \(\geq 400\) copies/mL (GS-US-380-4449). Full resistance criteria for each study are available [5-8]. All studies were undertaken in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocols were approved by independent review boards or ethics committees [5-8]. All participants provided written informed consent for the primary study analyses. ## 2.2. Genotypic data and resistance analyses Historical RNA or proviral DNA genotype reports for protease (PR), reverse transcriptase (RT), and integrase (IN) from local laboratories or commercial sites were included. Retrospective proviral DNA genotyping of PR/RT/IN using GenoSure Archive (Monogram Biosciences, CA, USA) was performed on baseline whole blood samples and a subset of Week 24 samples (GS-US-380-4580). Bioinformatic filters removed APOBEC-mediated, hypermutated deep-sequence reads from GenoSure Archive results to prevent RAM overreporting (e.g., E138K, M184I, and M230I in RT, and G163R in IN) as previously described [9]. Participant inclusion, RAM categorization, and statistical analysis ### 2.3.1. Longitudinal analysis Participants with historical and/or baseline proviral genotypic data from \(\geq 2\) timepoints prior to study drug initiation were included. Those with 2 genotype reports were included in the 2-timepoint analysis and those with \(\geq 3\) reports in the multiple-timepoint analysis. For the 2-timepoint analysis, substitutions were categorized as \(100\%\) detected (reported on both tests) or \(50\%\) detected (reported on test 1 or test 2 only). For the multiple-timepoint analysis, RAM detection was categorized as persistent (reported at all timepoints), lost (reported at first timepoint only), gained (reported at all timepoints, except the first), or inconsistent (reported intermittently). Differences between category counts were determined using Fisher exact test. Time between tests was reported as median (quartile [Q]1, Q3). Time between tests was compared using the Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn multiple comparisons or the Mann-Whitney \(U\) test. ### 2.3.2. Repeat archive testing Participants with 2-4 GenoSure Archive replicates from the same blood draw from baseline and/or Week 24 samples were included. Reproducibility \((\%)\) of RAMs and other substitutions (calculated as the number of times the mutation was detected per number of genotypic assays run) was reported as mean \(\pm\) standard deviation (SD). Wilcoxon rank-sum tests compared reproducibility between RAMs/substitutions groups, and a zero-truncated binomial model estimated the probability of RAM detection and its \(95\%\) confidence interval. # 3. Results ## 3.1. Longitudinal analysis ### 3.1.1. Participant clinical, demographic, and genotypic characteristics Overall, 241 participants (35 from GS-US-380-4449, 93 from GS-US-380-4030, and 113 from GS-US-380-4580) were included, with genotype reports collected from March 1997 to March 2019. At study initiation, most participants were male (76%; 184/241), Black (54%; 130/241), virologically suppressed (99%; 238/241), with HIV-1 subtype B (91%; 218/241); median (Q1, Q3) age was 52 (39, 61) years and CD4 count was 644 (465, 871) cells/μL (Supplemental Table 1). Genotypic data were available from 223 and 25 participants for the 2- and multiple-timepoint analyses, respectively (7 participants had IN data at 2 pre-switch timepoints and PR/RT data at \(\geq 3\) pre-switch timepoints and were included in both analyses). For the 2-timepoint analysis, 430 PR/RT and 140 IN reports were analyzed from 215 and 70 participants, respectively. The majority of IN reports were 1-3 years apart (69%; 48/70), and approximately half (48%; 104/215) of PR/RT reports were \(\geq 5\) years apart (Supplemental Table 2). For PR/RT genotypes, most comparisons were RNA to DNA (79%; 169/215) or DNA to DNA (20%; 44/215), with RNA to RNA occurring rarely (1%; 2/215). For IN, most reports compared DNA to DNA (66%; 46/70); the remaining were RNA to DNA (34%; 24/70). For the multiple-timepoint analysis, 98 reports (97 PR/RT and 5 IN) from 25 participants were included. Most reports (88%; 22/25) had \(\geq 5\) years between the first and last test (median [Q1, Q3] 9.3 [5.7, 14.4] years) (Supplemental Table 2). Participants had a median of 3 reports, most commonly RNA genotype (65%; 64/98); 96% (24/25) had \(\geq 1\) DNA genotype report. ### 3.1.2. Longitudinal 2-timepoint analysis: reporting patterns of primary RAMs and other substitutions Overall, 262 RAMs and 4866 other substitutions were analyzed. Of the 262 RAMs, 103 (39%) had \(100\%\) detection; 159 (61%) were detected \(50\%\) of the time, with 58 (37%) reported on the first test and 101 (64%) detected on the second test (Fig. 1; Table 2). The time between tests was similar between RAMs with \(100\%\) and \(50\%\) detection (median [Q1, Q3] 7.7 [3.2, 11.1] and 5.6 [3.1, 9.7] years, respectively) (Table 2). When analyzed by drug class, the categorization of RAMs was similar for protease inhibitor (PI), non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI), and nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) resistance (-R) (100% detection: 38%, 46%, and 31%, respectively; 50% detection: 63%, 54%, and 69%, respectively) (Fig. 1; Table 2). Detection patterns for specific RAMs are shown in Table 2. ### 3.1.3. Longitudinal multiple-timepoint analysis: reporting patterns of primary RAMs In total, 57 RAMs were analyzed and categorized as persistent (19%), lost (12%), gained (26%), or inconsistent (42%) (Table 3). Median (Q1, Q3) time between tests was 10.3 (1.8, 10.3), 14.6 (6.4, 15.3), 8.5 (5.1, 9.3), and 14.2 (6.9, 16.9) years for the persistent, lost, gained, and inconsistent categories, respectively, and was statistically similar between RAMs in all categories, except for gained versus inconsistent detection \((\mathfrak{p} = 0.0441)\) (Table 3). Detection patterns for the 24 RAMs categorized as inconsistently reported are detailed in Supplemental Table 3. ## 3.2. Repeat archive testing ### 3.2.1. Participant clinical and demographic characteristics Overall, from 70 participants (12 from GS-US-380-4449, 39 from GS-US-380-4030, and 19 from GS-US-380-4580), 90 whole blood samples from October 2016 to July 2019 were analyzed. Baseline and Week 24 samples were available from study GS-US-380-4580; one participant from study GS-US-380-4449 participated in a previous study (GS-US 292-1826) and samples from both studies were included. Two to four replicates were run for each sample, resulting in the analysis of 257 proviral genotype reports. Most participants were male (79%; 55/70), White (56%; 39/70), virologically suppressed (96%; 67/70), with HIV-1 subtype B (86%; 60/70); median (Q1, Q3) age was 57 (51, 65) years and CD4 count was 707 (473, 908) cells/μL (Supplemental Table 1). ### 3.2.2. Reproducibility of detection of primary RAMs and other substitutions Overall, 336 RAMs and 4399 other substitutions were documented. For primary RAMs, high reproducibility was generally observed (mean frequency [SD] \(80.9\%\) [27.2%]) and was similar across PI-R, NRTI-R, and NNRTI-R categories (mean frequencies \(77.9 - 83.5\%\) ) (Fig. 2; Table 4). While overall reproducibility was high, variability was observed for some substitutions (e.g., M184V in RT had a mean [SD] reproducibility of \(82.3\%\) [25.2%], with \(14\%\) of cases detected in 1/4 or 1/3 reports; \(23\%\) in 1/2, 2/4, 2/3, or 3/4 reports; and \(63\%\) in all reports) (Fig. 2; Table 4). Low reproducibility (mean [SD] \(51.4\%\) [29.1%]) was noted with INSTI RAMs; the very low number of RAMs \((n = 6)\) most likely contributed to this observation. Reproducibility for other RT substitutions was significantly higher than for primary NRTI and NNRTI RAMs \((86.0\%\) vs \(82.6\%\) and \(77.9\%\) respectively; \(p < 0.05\) for both comparisons) (Fig. 2; Table 4). Reproducibility of PI, NRTI, and NNRTI RAM detection was \(10 - 17\%\) higher when mutations were detected in RNA or proviral DNA historically, compared with those having no prior detection or no historical data \((p < 0.05\) for both comparisons) (Supplemental Fig. 1). By zero-truncated binomial modelling, if a participant had a PI, NRTI, or NNRTI RAM, the probability of it being reported by proviral genotyping was \(76 - 80\%\) (Supplemental Fig. 2); this increased to \(89\%\) if historically detected and decreased to \(59\%\) if not detected previously (Supplemental Fig. 2). Discussion This retrospective analysis characterized longitudinal patterns of RAM detection and reproducibility of proviral RAM detection from a single timepoint by utilizing genotypic data from 3 B/F/TAF switch studies. In the longitudinal 2-timepoint analysis, \(\sim 40\%\) of RAMs were detected at both timepoints. RAMs detected only once were mostly in the more recent sample. In the multiple-timepoint analysis, almost half of the RAMs were categorized as having inconsistent detection, with 12/24 detected in the most recent proviral DNA report. These data suggest that in the analysis timeframe, RAM frequency did not predominantly decay over time, and a lack of detection at a given timepoint does not indicate that the mutation is no longer present. Notably, the time between tests did not differ between the different detection categorizations, suggesting that persistence of RAMs could not be attributed to shorter intervals between reporting. Other more limited retrospective studies assessing NRTI and NNRTI RAM kinetics over time in virologically suppressed PWH have shown varying patterns of RAM detection in the latent reservoir [11-14]. Some studies demonstrated minimal change in detection between visits [12, 14], while others showed most RAMs were detected less frequently over time [11,13]. The persistence of RAM reporting was associated with the level and duration of HIV RNA replication under drug pressure, suggesting that when larger pools of circulating variants are present, the potential for mutations to be archived increases [11,12]. Drug pressure during virologic suppression was not linked to persistence of RAM detection [12]. This aligns with data demonstrating a lack of viral evolution during effective ART, suggesting that CD4 cell proliferation, rather than active viral replication, maintains the latent reservoir [15]. It is unknown whether the clinical characteristics of these participants drove the differences in RAM detection observed between studies. Despite reduced RAM detection in many participants over time, others showed documented continued resistance, with inconsistent, persistent, and emergent detection of RAMs [11-13]. The variability of RAM detection by proviral genotyping may be linked to the dynamic nature of the HIV latent reservoir, which expands and contracts over time as the pools of memory CD4 cells latently infected with HIV-1 variants are modulated in response to stimuli [4]. Additionally, while the reservoir size decreases during the first years of ART (half-life 44.2 months), there appears to be no further decrease afterwards, which may contribute to RAM persistence [16]. When examining the sensitivity of proviral genotyping by repeat testing, the reproducibility of primary RAM detection was \(\sim 80\%\) \((\pm \sim 25\%)\) , indicating that reporting of substitutions can be relatively high but variable. In addition to differences in the number of replicates and normal statistical variation, factors which may contribute to this variability include differences in plasma/archive kinetics. Importantly, the presence of a mutation can be confirmed even if reproducibility is low, but lack of repeated detection cannot confirm absence. Substitutions detected \(50\%\) of the time in the longitudinal analysis or with lower reproducibility in repeat archive testing may reflect rarer variants. Non-resistance substitutions were predominantly reported \(100\%\) of the time in the longitudinal analysis and had higher reproducibility of detection than RAMs in repeat archive testing. The robustness of detection of non-resistance substitutions may reflect greater stability compared to RAMs due to their negligible effect on viral fitness and potential to evade immune detection. A limitation of this study is that ART impact was not considered in the longitudinal analysis. Additionally, information regarding the impetus for generating historical genotypic reports was not available (i.e., whether testing was due to virologic failure). For instance, knowing whether the presence of RNA genotyping data was suggestive of treatment failure could improve understanding of whether newly reported RAMs were emergent or previously undocumented. However, even when excluding potential de novo resistance (50% detected, second report only), two-thirds of RAMs were still detected in both reports. Furthermore, this study included both RNA and DNA reports, and, as proviral DNA may harbor RAMs not detectable in plasma RNA, this could influence detection between tests [9]. For example, when M184V was detected only at the second timepoint, and RNA versus DNA reports were compared, reduced viral fitness could have led to reversion to wild-type after being archived in proviral DNA, thus rendering it undetectable in RNA tests, but detectable in proviral DNA tests. Of note, when 2 reports were available, M184V was persistently detected in over a quarter of cases; when there were multiple reports, M184V/I detection was mostly inconsistent, and loss of the mutation was rare. Technical details of the local and commercial assays were also not always available, and therefore a mix of sequencing methods (e.g., Sanger versus next-generation sequencing), and possibly a range of population sequencing reporting levels were analyzed. While harmonizing frequency of reporting may aid uniformity of RAM reporting, having different assays with potentially different cut-offs is a scenario that may be observed in clinical practice. Accordingly, these data help reinforce the recommendation that all prior and current drug-resistance genotypic and phenotypic test results are used, as not all RAMs may be detected at the time of testing [1]. Limited data are available regarding the predictive value of archived RAMs for ART efficacy. Utilizing a proviral DNA genotypic susceptibility score showed a higher probability of experiencing virologic rebound when virologically suppressed individuals had archived virus with intermediate or full resistance to \(\geq 1\) antiretroviral in their regimen [17]. A post hoc analysis of predictors of virologic failure in Phase 3 cabotegravir+rilpivirine studies identified archived rilpivirine resistance as a factor associated with virologic failure [18,19]. While the clinical relevance of archived resistance is not well defined, US DHHS guidelines recommend proviral DNA genotypic testing (if available) when optimizing or switching ART regimens in people with virologic suppression, especially when complex preexisting resistance is suspected, multiple prior failures have occurred, there is a prolonged history of prior ART regimens, and/or prior genotypic resistance test results are unavailable [1]. However, the decision to conduct proviral DNA genotypic testing may depend on several factors, including geographic region, prevalence of resistance, healthcare provider resources, and health insurance reimbursement policies, and may not be accessible to all PWH.
