emerging African literature is documenting an increasing incidence of DTG resistance, particularly in real-world settings, contrasting with data from controlled clinical trials [3]. In our previous study, we reported a suppression control rate among patient on DTG-based treatment very high (95%), which clearly demonstrates the success of such regimens; however, a growing body of literature is showing also the potential risk of the emergence of DTG-resistance in the African continent. Although the percentage of resistance remains relatively low, it could still translate into thousands of affected patients across the region.

In large randomized studies such as the NADIA trial (Uganda, Kenya, Zimbabwe) and the DAWNING trial, the rate of INSTI resistance emergence remained low (4% and 1%, respectively), thanks to intensive viral load monitoring and optimized therapeutic strategies [14, 15]. However, these conditions are rarely replicated in routine African healthcare contexts, where virological failures may go undetected for a long period of time. In real-world cohorts similar to ours, such as that reported by Ismael et al. in Mozambique, the prevalence of INSTI mutations among individuals with DTG failure reached  \(15 - 20\%\)  [16]; in other cohorts, with different selection criteria, the rates where even higher [17]. While these findings are concerning, current evidence does not allow us to determine whether the incidence of DTG resistance is truly increasing over time, or simply more frequently identified as resistance testing becomes more accessible and widely implemented.

The G118R and E138K mutations, each found in  \(43.8\%\)  of our resistant cases, are among the most frequently reported DTG resistance pathways in non-B subtypes, particularly subtype C, which was predominant in our sample. The relevance of G118R has been highlighted by several studies: the meta-analysis by Semengue et al. identified G118R and R263K as the most common INSTI mutations in African failures [7], while the review by Kamori and Barabona emphasized its selection in subtypes A and C, facilitated by its low fitness cost [5]. The  \(\mathrm{G118R + R263K}\)  combination, also observed in our study, has been associated with high-level resistance and reduced viral fitness [18], and biochemical studies [19] confirmed its preferential selection in subtype C.

Our study also reinforces the strong association between a complex treatment history and resistance risk. DTG-resistant participants had a significantly longer treatment history (median 15 years) and more frequent past failures. This is consistent with Loosli et al., who reported similar patterns in a large African-European cohort [6]. Furthermore, we observed INSTI mutations even in participants who were DTG-naive or had initiated the drug while virologically suppressed. This finding are in line with reports from Mahomed et al., Fourie et

al., and Mens et al., where G118R emerged under conditions of suboptimal adherence or functionally ineffective regimens [20-22].

The observed co-resistance patterns—particularly the frequent presence of M184V and K65R—highlight the threat of multi-drug resistance in individuals failing DTG-based regimens, even in the absence of PI resistance. This pattern mirrors findings from other papers who reported NNRTI and NRTI resistance in participants failing DTG-based therapy [16, 17]. Our results therefore reinforce the concern that switching to DTG without assessing virological suppression may lead to resistance selection on a background of already compromised backbones.

Lastly, our findings take on special relevance considering the growing interest in long-acting therapies such as cabotegravir. The G118R mutation, also observed in our study, has been associated with reduced susceptibility to cabotegravir in vitro, raising concerns about cross-resistance [5, 23]. The editorial by Fokam et al. in Nature Medicine strongly advocates for integrating resistance testing into routine clinical care in low-income countries to avoid silent accumulation of INSTI mutations. Similarly, the review by Tao et al. emphasizes that persistent, unrecognized viremia is a key driver of resistance emergence even in ART-naive individuals, a situation reflected in our cohort [24].

### Limitations

This study has several limitations. First, due to the small number of participants included  \((n = 28)\)  and the fact that genotypic resistance testing was not performed systematically on all individuals with virological failure, the epidemiological value of our prevalence estimates is limited.

Second, resistance testing was restricted to the integrase region only for about half of the samples, additional mutations in other regions (e.g., protease or reverse transcriptase) might have gone undetected in participants not fully sequenced. Moreover, Stanford scores were available only for a subset of individuals, precluding systematic classification of resistance levels across the full sample.

Finally, data on viral load trajectories, adherence, and treatment history were incomplete for some participants, limiting the capacity to reconstruct the exact pathway leading to the emergence of resistance in each case. Despite these limitations, our study provides important early signals on the possible patterns of DTG resistance in real-world Mozambican settings and highlights the urgent need for expanded molecular surveillance.

### Public Health Implications

The findings of this study could have implications for public health policy and HIV program implementation in sub-Saharan Africa. First, the emergence of DTG

resistance—even among participants initiating treatment while virally suppressed—highlights the need to revise current "test-and-switch" strategies. We are aware of the effectiveness of DTG-based regimens, but we argue that virological monitoring and resistance testing should be strengthened prior to transitioning individuals to DTG-based regimens, especially in settings with a history of limited adherence or prior treatment failures. In the actual guidelines, WHO recommends the availability of genotyping testing only in context in which DTG-based regimens are not available; our results, together with other similar data, suggest the need to revise this recommendation, and make resistance testing more available on the field, in Africa, too.

For these reasons, our data underscore the urgency of integrating genotypic resistance testing into national HIV guidelines and decentralizing access to such diagnostics. Establishing sentinel surveillance systems in high-prevalence areas could allow for early detection of resistance trends and inform timely changes in treatment protocols.

Finally, the potential for cross-resistance to newer long-acting therapies such as cabotegravir calls for cautious and evidence-based scale-up of such interventions, considering also the extensive resistance to NNRTI typically present in individuals having failed first generation NNRTI regimens [3], that might affect the efficacy of rilpivirine (the second drug present in the long-acting regimen). Investments in molecular diagnostic capacity and targeted training of healthcare workers are essential to ensure that therapeutic innovations do not inadvertently accelerate resistance at the population level.

In summary, our data confirm and expand on recent African evidence regarding DTG resistance: G118R, E138K, R263K, and L74M represent emerging mutational patterns in Mozambique, particularly among individuals with extensive treatment history, unsuppressed viral load, or prior failures. The possible spread of such mutations, even in clinically stable individuals, may have implications for the long-term sustainability of DTG-based regimens and highlights the need to implement sentinel genotypic surveillance strategies in public treatment programs.

## Conclusion

This retrospective analysis describes the presence of integrase inhibitor resistance mutations among individuals with virological failure on DTG-based ART in five DREAM centers in Mozambique. Among those tested, nearly half showed evidence of resistance, with a predominance of G118R and other mutations previously associated with DTG failure in non-B subtypes. The findings reflect the need for ongoing monitoring of DTG resistance in routine programmatic settings and support the value of implementing targeted genotypic surveillance

where feasible. Further studies with systematic sampling will be important to better estimate the prevalence and clinical implications of resistance in similar contexts.

Second-line regimens are PI/r (ATV/r or LPV/r) plus optimized NRTI backbone while third-line include regimens containing either DTG and/or DRV/r and/or NRTI (usually selected based on a genotypic resistance test). Treatment failure is defined as two consecutive viral loads \(\geq 1000\) copies/ml following at least six months of antiretroviral therapy, with enhanced adherence counselling. Percentage of individuals with a genotypic susceptibility score (GSS) of \(< 30\) on Stanford were considered to preserve potential efficacy while those with a GSS score of \(\geq 30\) were considered to have limited activity. #### Data management and statistical analysis Centre for disease control (CDC) Epi info version 7.2.6. was used for statistical analysis following data verification, cleaning and validation. The mean and standard deviation (SD) or median and inter-quartile range (IQR) were used for quantitative variables. Chi square/Fisher exact tests were used to compare categorical variables, while Student T test was used to compare continuous variables between groups. P values \(< 0.05\) were considered statistically significant. Any variables with p values \(< 0.2\) on bivariate analyses were eligible for multivariate analysis. ### Results #### Characteristics of study participants Of 2109 individuals assessed, 203 met inclusion criteria, median age 37 [16-47] years and 118/203 (58.13%) females. The median [IQR] duration on ART was 10 [6.9-13.3] years, with majority (160, 78.70%) on second-line, 34 (16.80%) on first-line and 9 (4.50%) on third-line. Detailed regimens included: ABC + 3TC + EFV/NVP (0.98%); AZT + 3TC + EFV/NVP (1.47) TDF + 3TC + EFV/NVP (6.89%); TDF + 3TC + DTG (7.39%%); AZT + 3TC + DTG (0.49%); ABC + 3TC + DTG (3.94%); ABC + 3TC + ATV/r (17.73%); ABC + 3TC + LPV/r (6.40%); AZT + 3TC + ATV/r (15.76%), AZT + 3TC + LVP/r (5.42%); TDF + 3TC + ATV/r (29.56%); TDF + 3TC + LPV/r (3.94%). Overall, median [IQR] viral load was 46,000 [8,480-194,487] copies/ml and median [IQR] CD4 count was 239.50 [125-452] cells/μl. The median viral load was comparable after first (929,837 [7,309-132,270] copies/ml), second- (51,451 [9,632-204,463] copies/ml) and third-line failure (37,415 [8,930-369,430] copies/ml), \(p = 0.7\) . The median CD4 count was higher at first-line failure (406 [184-642] cells/μl) as compared to second-line failure (214.5 [103-394] cells/μl), \(p = 0.03\) , while there was limited CD4 data in those failing third-line. Table 1 shows characteristics of participants. #### HIV genotypic and resistance profiles HIVDR rates are summarized in Table 2. Overall HIVDR (presence of at least one HIVDR resistance mutation) was \(87.19\%\) (177/203). NRTI-NNRTI dual class resistance was similar in first- and second-line \((p = 0.842)\) , while triple-class resistance was higher in second-line as compared to first-line \((p < 0.0001)\) . The most prevalent viral clade was CRF02_AG (119 (58.60%)), followed by G (19 (9.36%)), A \(_1\) (18 (8.87%), F2 (11(5.42%), D (8(3.94%), CRF01_AE (5(2.46%)), CRF18_cpx (5(2.46%), CRF06_cpx (3(1.48%), CRF11_cpx (3(1.48%), CRF22_01A1 (3(1.48%), CRF13_cpx (2(0.99%), CRF37_cpx (2(0.99%), H (1(0.49%) and G/D (1(0.49%) while three individuals (1.48%) harboured HIV-1 group O. #### Mutational profiles Mutational profiles are summarized in Fig. 1 (panel A, B and C). M184V mutation most prevalent among NRTI mutations \((65.52\%)\) , followed by the thymidine analogue mutation (TAM), M41L \((24.14\%)\) . Among NNRTI mutations, K103N was most prevalent \((35.96\%)\) , followed by A98G \((18.72\%)\) . Among PI/r mutations, M46I \((19.70\%)\) , was most prevalent followed by F53L \((12.81\%)\) . #### Factors associated with HIVDR Table 3 summarizes factors associated to HIV drug resistance (HIVDR). Neither age, gender, line of treatment, WHO clinical stage, viral load, CD4 count, nor genetic diversity were significantly associated with HIVDR \((p > 0.05)\) #### Potentially active drugs Potentially active drugs after ART-failure are shown in Fig. 2 (Fig. 2A and B). Supplementary figure Panel B shows potentially active drugs that could accompany and/or substitute DTG and other INSTIs in patients failing DTG containing First-line and second-line regimens. ### Discussion We herein describe ADR patterns in ART-failing PWH in Cameroon. Although some data has previously been reported in this context, last reports were in the pre-DTG era, collected between 2011 and 2019 [14]. The current study gives an update on ADR, necessary to guide treatment options here and in similar RLS with limited laboratory capacity for GRT in ART-failing individuals [25]. Performed in the context DTG-roll-out, this update is of added relevance as it describes optimal accompanying regimens in DTG-failing failing individuals initially naive to INSTI, increasing our chances for sustainability of DTG-based regimens. Lastly, given the continuous need for novel drugs in this context (such as second generation ![](images/10c7bbecaa0daa67faa7b9a5556e144d8556f81c9178ee3f4fe35d13998c915b.jpg) Fig. 1 HIVDR mutational profile of participants. A describes the mutational profiles in the entire population \((n = 203)\) ; B describes mutational profiles in individuals failing first-line antiretroviral therapy regimens \((n = 34)\) and C describes mutational profiles in individuals failing second-line antiretroviral regimens \((n = 160)\) . N.B. Only major mutations according to the Stanford HIV Drug Resistance database were described. (https://hivdb.stanford.edu/) NNRTI, capsid inhibitors, nucleoside reverse transcriptase translocation inhibitors), our findings could help inform strategies around selecting eligible candidates for these therapies. The overall high rate of HIVDR observed herein underscores its role as a major cause of virological failure, aligning with previous findings in similar populations [11]. HIVDR in this context is driven by limited treatment options, low genetic barrier regimens, poor adherence, inadequate viral load monitoring and delayed detection of treatment failure and resistance [26]. Indeed duration of treatment was long in this population (often associated to higher rates of HIVDR) [11], with poor immunovirological status, especially after second line failure, suggesting higher disease progression [26]. Proper monitoring strategies for viral load, CD4 count and GRT in this setting would enable timely detection of failure, reducing the risks of HIVDR accumulation and disease progression [27]. HIVDR rates were highest for NNRTIs, followed by NRTI and lastly PI/r [27]. Also, high rates of NNRTI and NRTI resistance were observed as from first-line failure, again calling for adequate monitoring to enable timely detection of failure, and potential benefits for GRT even as from first-line failure [26], though some studies suggest limited benefits of GRT in first-line failures [28]. Nonetheless, this could help preserve NRTI accompanying molecules used in first-line for use in subsequent ART-regimens [29]. Indeed, HIV-related morbidity and mortality remains worrying in paediatrics in this setting. In this study, all children aged 0–9 years and \(83.1\%\) of children aged 10–19 harboured a virus with at least one HIVDR mutation. Children and adolescents face additional challenges linked to social/psychological, drug dosing and formulations, poorer adherence, risks of TDR and PDR (especially to first generation NNRTI) and high viral loads at diagnosis and failure, which may all increase risks of HIVDR at failure, necessitating adapted strategies for optimal treatment outcomes [31–33]. Lastly, about \(37.0\%\) of our population had NRTI-NNRTI-PI/r triple-class resistance, raising the need for introduction of novel drug regimens with different mechanisms of action. With respect to mutational profiles, the M184V mutation was most prevalent. Though this causes high resistance to 3TC/FTC, it potentializes AZT and TDF, while reducing viral replicative fitness. For this reason, 3TC/FTC are usually maintained in ART regimens despite M184V, which also serves as an adherence marker [34-37]. Both type I and II TAMs were present, causing varying levels of cross-resistance to ABC and TDF (higher in the case of type I TAMs), with potential to jeopardize ART-regimens even in individuals without previous exposure to ABC/TDF [38]. This leaves the possibility for suboptimal second-line-ART, with blind use of ABC/TDF, as poor documentation of treatment ![](images/59bfe0e86305787b18c9adc9757ea8389dc64ddef7e646e0405de29353435e3a.jpg) 2A: Potentially active drugs after First-line treatment failure. Fig. 2 Potentially active drugs after first-line treatment failure (A) and second-line treatment failure (B) ![](images/6ce2d416509a2648e9e055ac9091d35bfe89243d517902e58ee8edf1a2289876.jpg) 2B: Potentially active drugs after Second-line treatment failure. histories/records and medical nomadism are frequent in this context. GRT use may be of importance in such cases to identify unpredicted resistance/cross-resistance. The K103N mutation was most frequent among NNRTIs, confirming limited potential for recycling first generation NNRTIs [39]. Meanwhile, mutations causing cross-resistance to second generation NNRTI (Y181C, K101E/P, G190A, Y188L, M230L, and V106A) were frequent, with only about \(50\%\) of individuals preserving potential efficacy each to DOR, ETR or RPV after first-line, calling for careful considerations around the potential use of second-generation NNRTI (such as in acting and dual-ART regimens) [40]. This should take into account extensive exposure to first-generation NNRTI, high rates of NNRTI resistance in ART-failing individuals, and therefore the potential of archived NNRTI resistance in viral reservoirs, with potential to affect such therapeutic options [41-43]. Overall, PI/r resistance was lowest, supporting their use in second and third line (DRV/r) regimens [44], with the possibility of recycling ATV/r and LPV/r even after second line failure if helped by resistance testing. The main limitation of this study was the inability to sequence of the integrase region in individuals on DTG-based regimens at the time of the study. It is worth noting that INSTI were introduced into Cameroonian guidelines (in first- or third-line regimens) only as from 2020 [24]. Therefore, GRT only involved the RT and PR regions, till recently when we developed a sequencing protocol for integrase sequencing [45], which was however not readily available yet for routine management at this time. Nonetheless, it is worth noting that integrase HIVDR remains rare in real world practice, occurring usually in some high-risk clinical scenarios, such as previous exposure to INSTI (which is not the case in this setting), use of DTG as mono or dual therapy, concomitant treatment with rifampicin or presence of resistance to NRTI accompanying molecules [46]. The few individuals on INSTI-based regimens here (24 out of 203) were at low risk of developing INSTI resistance. Furthermore, based on our studies carried out around the same period, there was high baseline efficacy of DTG, and little effect of DRMs on treatment response [5, 21, 31]. Indeed, of the 24 individuals, 15 were using DTG as first-line regimens, a population in which INSTI resistance is rare [32, 48]. To add, the median duration on DTG-based regimens was low (about one year) and resistance to NRTI and PI/r accompanying molecules in these individuals was also low (supplementary figure Panel A), suggesting preserved efficacies of DTG, favoured by its high genetic barrier and forgiveness to non-observance. To add, no individual had the K65R mutation (even though 23/24 of them used either ABC/3TC or TDF/3TC as accompanying molecules), again suggesting preserved efficacy of DTG. The unsuppressed viral loads in these individuals would therefore have been driven mainly by poor adherence to therapy. Lastly, recent findings have shown high rates of efficacy of DTG based regimens, even despite presence of resistance to accompanying NRTI molecules, although more data in clinical contexts is needed with respect to this [47, 49]. Another limitation is the use of conventional sanger sequencing, which limited our ability to detect minority viral populations, which have recently shown clinical relevance. Lastly, in the public health approach, the threshold for virological failure and eligibility for resistance testing was a viral load \(\geq 1000\) copies/ml making it possible for some resistance cases below 1000 copies/ml being missed [5]. Nonetheless, our study aligns with the current standard of care in this context and similar settings. ### Conclusion In this population with long duration on ART, poor immune-virological status and late detection of failure, ADR levels are high, and driven mostly by NNRTI resistance, supporting the use of NNRTI-sparing ART and careful considerations around the introduction of second generation NNRTI. All PI/r appear suitable for switch to second line while DRV/r remains active for switching to third-line ART, though some patterns after second line failure are complex, including triple-class resistance. Our findings underline the necessity for improved access to viral load and CD4 monitoring to enable opportune detection of failure, improved access and use of genotypic resistance testing (including newer drug targets such as integrase) to enable sustainable ART, and the need for introduction of new ARV drugs with novel mechanisms of action. These measures would significantly contribute to eliminating the HIV/AIDS pandemic by 2030. ### Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12981-025-00775-z. **Study Objectives**
The objective of this project is to systematically extract and curate data related to HIV drug resistance from published reports. For each paper, identify and summarize information on:

1. HIV nucleotide or amino-acid sequences obtained from clinical samples, including GenBank accession numbers.
2. The populations from whom HIV sequences were obtained.
3. The clinical samples and sequencing methods used.
4. Antiretroviral \(ARV\) treatment histories of the individuals whose samples were sequenced.

**Question 1 – Does the paper report HIV sequences from patient samples?**
**Goal:** Determine whether the study generated new HIV nucleotide or amino-acid sequences, or reported lists of mutations, directly from clinical samples obtained from individuals with HIV \(ART-naïve or ART-experienced\).
**Answer “Yes” if the paper:**

- States that genetic sequencing, genotypic resistance testing, Sanger sequencing, next-generation sequencing, or single-genome sequencing was performed on clinical samples such as plasma, serum, PBMCs, proviral DNA, or dried blood spots.
- Indicates that sequencing was done on samples from patients, participants, subjects, blood donors, newly diagnosed or newly infected individuals, PLWH/PWH, or cohorts of individuals with HIV.
- States that surveillance for transmitted or acquired drug resistance was performed and generated new sequence data.
- Reports GenBank accession numbers for sequences generated in the study.

**Answer “No” if:**

- Only laboratory strains \(e.g., HXB2, IIIB, NL4-3, BAL, LAI\) or site-directed mutants were studied.
- The paper is a review or meta-analysis using sequences reported in other studies or downloaded from databases without generating new sequences.

**Question 2 – Does the paper report in vitro drug susceptibility data?**
**Goal:** Determine whether the paper quantifies HIV in vitro susceptibility to ARV drugs.
**Answer “Yes” if the paper:**

- States that phenotypic susceptibility testing, phenotypic resistance testing, or a drug susceptibility assay was performed.
- Reports IC₅₀, EC₅₀, EC₉₀, fold change in susceptibility, or similar measures.
- Describes a susceptibility assay \(e.g., PhenoSense/Monogram, Antivirogram/Virco\) or gives details on cells, drug titrations, and reporter readouts.
- Specifies the virus used for testing \(e.g., clinical isolate, site-directed mutant, virus from in vitro passage\).

Otherwise, answer “No”.

**Question 3 – Were sequences from the paper made publicly available?**
**Goal:** Determine whether newly generated HIV sequences or raw reads were deposited in public repositories \(e.g., GenBank, SRA, DDBJ, ENA\).
**Answer “Yes” if the paper:**

- Provides GenBank accession numbers \(typically two letters followed by digits\) in the Methods, Results, a Supplementary Table, or Data Availability statement.
- States that sequences have been submitted to GenBank or another public database, even if accession numbers are “pending.”
- States that raw reads are available in SRA or other sequence-read repositories.

**Answer “No” if:**

- Only accession numbers for HIV reference strains \(e.g., HXB2, NL4-3, LAI, BAL\) are given.
- No accession numbers or deposition statements are provided.
- Only accession numbers from previous studies are cited.
- The paper is a review or meta-analysis using existing sequence data.

**Question 4 – What are the GenBank accession numbers for sequenced HIV isolates?**

- If the paper reports that sequences were submitted to GenBank or another public database and provides accession numbers, extract all individual accession numbers and ranges \(e.g., FJ800379–FJ800386; GQ477441–GQ477451; KP170487\).
- Accession numbers may appear in the Methods, in a table, in Supplementary material, or in a Data Availability statement.
- If accession numbers are described but extraction is ambiguous, copy the relevant text describing the submission.

If no accession numbers are given, answer “Not reported”.

**Question 5 – How many individuals had samples obtained for HIV sequencing?**

- If the paper does **not** report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, or only compiles sequences from databases/previous studies, answer **0**.
- If sequencing or genotypic resistance testing was performed on samples or sequences from X individuals, answer **X**.
- If the paper reports X isolates/sequences from a group of patients but does not specify how many individuals contributed isolates, assume one sequence per individual and answer **X**, unless stated otherwise.
- If multiple mutually exclusive patient groups are described, sum individuals across all groups.
- If sequences were generated but the number of individuals is not reported, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 6 – From which countries were the sequenced samples obtained?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, answer **“Not applicable”**.
- Use the country or countries where samples were collected \(e.g., recruitment, enrollment, follow-up, or surveillance site\).
- If multiple countries are listed, report all.
- If samples were collected in country A and sequenced in country B, report **country A**.
- If no country information is provided, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 7 – From what years were the sequenced samples obtained?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, answer **“Not applicable”**.
- If sample collection dates are reported \(e.g., Year1–Year2, or month/year ranges\), report the year span \(e.g., “June 2004–April 2007” → **2004–2007**\).
- If samples are listed by individual years \(e.g., 2008, 2009, 2010\), report the full span \(e.g., **2008–2010**\).
- If only months within a single year are reported \(e.g., March–September 2008\), report that single year \(**2008**\).
- If baseline sequencing corresponds to enrollment or diagnosis years, use that year range.
- If no sample-collection years are provided, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 8 – Were samples cloned prior to sequencing?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV **or** does not report in vitro susceptibility data, answer **“Not applicable”**.
- Answer **“Yes”** if:
    - The paper states that “amplicons were cloned and sequenced,” or describes use of a cloning method \(e.g., TA/Topo TA cloning\).
    - Molecular clones were sequenced.
    - Single-genome amplification or limiting dilution was performed prior to sequencing.
    - Site-directed mutagenesis was performed on isolates that were sequenced.
- Answer **“No”** if:
    - Direct PCR or population-based sequencing is reported.
    - A commercial genotyping platform \(e.g., ViroSeq, TruGene, GeneSeqR, GenoSure, Vela Diagnostics\) is used.
    - Next-generation sequencing \(NGS\) without cloning is used.
- If cloning information is not provided, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 9 – Which HIV genes were reported to have been sequenced?**
Report all applicable gene targets using the abbreviations **PR**, **RT**, **IN**, **Pol**, **CA** \(capsid\), and **Env**.

- If the paper states “pol genotyping/sequencing” without further detail, answer **“Pol”**.
- If “protease and reverse transcriptase,” “PR/RT,” “ViroSeq,” or “TruGene \(PR/RT\)” are mentioned, include **PR** and **RT**.
- If “integrase,” “IN,” “GeneSeq/ViroSeq Integrase,” “INSTI resistance,” or “integrase sequencing” are mentioned, include **IN**.
- If NRTI or NNRTI resistance is assessed, include **RT**.
- If PI resistance is assessed, include **PR**.
- If INSTI resistance is assessed, include **IN**.
- If lenacapavir resistance is assessed, include **CA** \(capsid\).
- If “env,” “gp120,” “gp41,” “gp160,” “V3 loop/C2V3,” or coreceptor-usage genotyping is reported, include **Env**.

**Question 10 – What method was used for sequencing?**

- Answer **“Sanger sequencing”** if:
    - Dideoxy \(dideoxyterminator\) or Sanger sequencing is explicitly mentioned.
    - ABI or Thermo Fisher sequencing reagents/instruments are used.
    - Capillary electrophoresis, electropherograms, or “direct PCR sequencing” are described.
    - The paper was published before 2008 \(NGS was not widely used\).
- Answer **“NGS”** if:
    - “Next-generation sequencing,” “NGS,” or “ultra-deep sequencing” is reported.
    - Illumina platforms \(MiSeq, HiSeq, iSeq\), Oxford Nanopore \(e.g., GridION\), PacBio RSII/SMRT, 454 pyrosequencing, Sentosa, or Vela NGS systems are used.
- If the sequencing method is not described, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 11 – What type of samples were sequenced?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, answer **“Not applicable”**.
- If viral RNA was extracted from plasma or serum, include **“Plasma”**.
- If samples were obtained at diagnosis or at virological failure, they are likely plasma: include **“Plasma”**.
- If PBMCs, peripheral blood mononuclear cells, or proviral DNA are mentioned, include **“PBMC”**.
- If samples were from individuals with stable virological suppression, they are often PBMCs: include **“PBMC”**.
- If nucleic acids were extracted from whole blood, include **“Whole blood”**.
- If dried blood spots are used, include **“DBS”**.
- If other sample types \(e.g., lymph node, cerebrospinal fluid\) are used, list those specifically.
- If the specimen type for sequencing is not stated, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 12 – Were any sequences obtained from individuals with virological failure on a treatment regimen?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, answer **“Not applicable”**.
- Answer **“Yes”** if:
    - Samples were from patients with virological failure or virological rebound.
    - Sequencing was performed on plasma from ART-experienced individuals.
    - Samples were obtained from patients on second-line treatment.
    - Patients had received NRTIs, NNRTIs, PIs, and/or INSTIs and sequences were generated.
- Answer **“No”** if:
    - All sequenced patients were newly diagnosed or ART-naïve.
    - Sequencing was done exclusively for transmitted drug-resistance surveillance \(i.e., untreated individuals\).

**Question 13 – Were the patients in the study in a clinical trial?**

- Answer **“Yes”** if the paper:
    - Describes randomization to different treatments.
    - Describes a study as double-blind, placebo-controlled, open-label, controlled, or multicenter.
    - Describes a phase 1, 2, or 3 trial.
- Answer **“No”** if the paper:
    - Describes an observational or prospective cohort, retrospective or cross-sectional study, case-control study, or case series.
    - Provides no information suggesting clinical-trial participation.

**Note:** Registration at ClinicalTrials.gov \(NCT number\) alone is not sufficient to classify a study as a clinical trial.

**Question 14 – Does the paper report HIV sequences from individuals who had previously received ARV drugs?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, answer **“No”**.

# Final efficacy and safety of twice-yearly subcutaneous lenacapavir in treatment-naive people with HIV: randomized study



# Abstract

Objective: To assess final efficacy (through Week [W] 132), safety, and emergent resistance with lenacapavir-based combination regimens in the CALIBRATE study.

Design. CALIBRATE was a Phase 2, randomized, open-label study (NCT04143594).

Methods. Treatment-naive PWH were randomized (2:2:2:1) to four treatment groups (TG): TG1 and TG2 received twice-yearly subcutaneous lenacapavir plus oral daily emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (F/TAF); TG3 received oral daily lenacapavir plus F/TAF; and TG4 received oral daily bictegravir/F/TAF. At W28, TG1 switched to lenacapavir plus TAF and TG2 switched to lenacapavir plus bictegravir. At W80, TG4 completed the study and TG1-3 continued assigned treatments.

Results. Overall, 182 participants received  \(\geq 1\)  dose of study drug (TG1-4, respectively:  \(n = 52\) ,  \(n = 53\) ,  \(n = 52\) ,  \(n = 25\) ). Virologic suppression (HIV-1 RNA  \(< 50\)  copies/mL) at W80 by FDA snapshot:  \(87\%\) ,  \(75\%\) ,  \(87\%\) , and  \(92\%\)  in TG1-4, respectively. When excluding missing data, virologic suppression at W132 across TG1-3 was  \(98 - 100\%\) . Mean (95% CI) increase from baseline to W80 in CD4 cells/ \(\mu\) L was consistent across TG1-4: 275 (214; 337), 262 (203; 320), 245 (174; 315), and 248 (155; 340), respectively. No serious treatment-related adverse events occurred. Two participants in TG1 and three in TG2 discontinued study drug due to adverse events. Injection-site reactions were mostly mild to moderate. LEN resistance-associated mutations emerged in four participants.

Conclusions. Lenacapavir-containing combinations achieved and maintained high rates of virologic suppression in treatment-naive participants through W132; lenacapavir was well tolerated. These data support future development of lenacapavir-containing regimens for HIV-1 treatment.

# METHODS

## Study Design and Population

CALIBRATE was a Phase 2, randomized, open-label, active-controlled, multicenter study. Treatment-naive PwH were enrolled across 41 sites in the USA and Dominican Republic (study design presented in Fig. 1). Full methodologic details for CALIBRATE have been reported previously [11].

This study was approved by the institutional review board or ethics committee at all sites and was conducted in compliance with international laws and guidelines. Eligible participants were treatment naïve, ≥18 years old, and had screening plasma HIV-1 RNA of ≥200 copies/mL and CD4 cell counts of ≥200 cells/μL without active hepatitis B or C infection. All participants provided written informed consent.

## Procedures

Eligible participants were randomized (2:2:2:1) to one of four open-label treatment groups (TGs; TG1-4) by the investigator or designee using an interactive web response system, stratified by HIV-1 RNA ( \(\leq 100000\)  copies/mL or  \(>100000\)  copies/mL) at screening. Participants in TG1 and TG2 received SC LEN  \((927\mathrm{mg})\)  plus oral daily emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (F/TAF)  \((200/25\mathrm{mg})\)  for 28 weeks, and then switched from F/TAF to maintenance oral daily TAF  \((25\mathrm{mg})\)  (TG1) and oral daily bicegravir  \((75\mathrm{mg})\)  (TG2). TG3 received oral daily LEN  \((50\mathrm{mg})\)  with F/TAF  \((200/25\mathrm{mg})\)  and TG4 received an active control regimen of oral daily bicegravir  \((50\mathrm{mg})\)  with F/TAF  \((200/25\mathrm{mg})\)  (Fig. 1). After Week 80, participants in TG4 completed the study. Participants in TG1-3 could continue their assigned treatment from Week 80 onwards and attend clinic visits alternating between every 10 and 16 weeks until the product became accessible through an access program, or the study sponsor elected to discontinue the study in the country. Participants in TG1 and TG2 required oral bridging if an SC injection of LEN could not be administered within the protocol visit window; results from these participants have been reported elsewhere [18].

### Endpoints and Assessments

The primary endpoint was the proportion of participants with HIV-1 RNA  \(< 50\)  copies/mL at Week 54, as determined by FDA snapshot algorithm [19]. Pre-specified secondary efficacy endpoints included the proportion of participants with HIV-1 RNA  \(< 50\)  copies/mL per FDA snapshot algorithm at Week 80, and changes from baseline in HIV-1 RNA and CD4 cell count. Other efficacy endpoints included the proportion of participants with HIV-1 RNA  \(< 50\)  copies/mL by missing=failure and missing=excluded analyses. Full details on these analyses can be found in the Supplementary Methods, http://links.lww.com/QAD/D691.

Safety secondary endpoints included incidences of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAE) and graded laboratory abnormalities. Safety assessments included monitoring of AEs and concomitant medications, clinical laboratory analyses, vital sign measurements, electrocardiograms, and physical examinations. AEs were coded according to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (Version 23.1).

Emergence of LEN resistance was an exploratory endpoint. HIV-1 capsid genotypic and phenotypic data were assessed at study entry using the GenoSure Gag-Pro and PhenoSense Gag-Pro assays (Monogram Biosciences). Resistance testing was performed for any participants who met one of the following virologic failure criteria: suboptimal virological response, defined as two consecutive visits with HIV-1 RNA  \(\geq 50\)  copies/mL and a decline of  \(< 1\log_{10}\)  from Day 1 to Week 10; virological rebound, defined as two consecutive visits with HIV-1 RNA  \(\geq 50\)  copies/mL after reaching  \(< 50\)  copies/mL, or two consecutive visits with an increase from nadir of  \(>1\log_{10}\) ; or participants with HIV-1 RNA  \(\geq 50\)  copies/mL at last study visit.

### Statistical Analysis

This analysis included efficacy data up to Week 132, and safety and resistance data until the last study visit for each participant, which may have been up to Week 184. For the LEN-containing groups (TGs 1-3), a sample size of 50 participants was selected to estimate the response rate of HIV-1 RNA  \(< 50\)  copies/mL at Week 54, based on practical consideration and previous experiences for similar studies. To gather more safety data for LEN, each LEN-containing group was assigned double the participants of the control group. Analyses of the secondary efficacy and safety endpoints included all participants who were randomly assigned and received  \(\geq 1\)  dose of study drug. Incidence of TEAEs and laboratory abnormalities were summarized using descriptive statistics. The resistance analysis population (RAP) included any participant who received  \(\geq 1\)  dose of study drug and met  \(\geq 1\)  of the virologic failure criteria. For the proportion of participants with HIV-1 RNA  \(< 50\)  copies/mL per FDA snapshot algorithm, missing=excluded analysis, and missing=failure analysis at Week 80, point estimates and  \(95\%\)  confidence intervals (CIs) were constructed for comparisons of LEN-containing TGs with TG4 using stratum-adjusted Mantel-Haenszel proportion, stratified by baseline HIV-1 RNA level ( \(\leq 100000\)  or  \(>100000\)  copies/mL). The associated  \(P\) -values were estimated based on the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test stratified by baseline HIV-1 RNA level ( \(\leq 100000\)  copies/mL or  \(>100000\)  copies/mL). Differences in changes from baseline in  \(\log_{10}\)  HIV-1 RNA and CD4 cell count between LEN-containing TGs with TG4 and the associated  \(P\) -values and  \(95\%\)  CIs were constructed using analysis of variance models adjusting for baseline HIV-1 RNA level ( \(\leq 100000\)  copies/mL or  \(>100000\)  copies/mL).

# RESULTS

## Study Participants

Between 22 November 2019 and 27 August 2020, 183 participants in CALIBRATE were randomly assigned to one of four TGs. Overall, 182 participants received  \(\geq 1\)  dose of study drug (TG1,  \(n = 52\) ; TG2,  \(n = 53\) ; TG3,  \(n = 52\) ; TG4,  \(n = 25\) ; Supplementary Fig. 1, http://links.lww.com/QAD/D691). One participant was randomized, but did not receive study drug. Of the 183 participants enrolled at baseline, 130 (71%) participants continued treatment post Week 80, and 116 (63%) remained in the study through Week 132.

Baseline characteristics were generally balanced between TGs (Supplementary Table 1, http://links.lww.com/QAD/D691). Participants were mostly male (93%), had HIV-1 RNA of  \(\leq 100,000\)  copies/mL at baseline (85%), and CD4 counts of  \(\geq 350\)  cells/μL (69%). Median (interquartile range [IQR]) age was 29 (24–36), and over half of all participants were Black (52%).

## Efficacy

Virologic suppression (<50 copies/mL) at Week 80 by FDA snapshot algorithm was 45/52 (87%) in TG1, 40/53 (75%) in TG2, 45/52 (87%) in TG3, and 23/25 (92%) in TG4 (Fig. 2). At Week 80, when missing data were excluded, virologic suppression was similar across all groups (98–100%; Fig. 3A). No statistical difference was seen between TGs at Week 80 when missing data were excluded; percentage difference (95% CI) in virologic suppression versus TG4 was -2.8 (-12.8; 7.2:  \(P = .37\) ) for TG1 and -2.1 (-11.9; 7.7:  \(P = .48\) ) for TG3, virologic suppression in TG2 and TG4 at Week 80 was 100%. Virologic suppression remained similar across TG1–3 through Week 132 when missing data were excluded: TG1: 40/41 (98%); TG2: 39/39, (100%); TG3: 36/36, (100%); Fig. 3A). TG4 ended at Week 80. Virologic suppression when missing data were treated as virologic failure is reported in Supplementary Fig. 2, http://links.lww.com/QAD/D691. By Week 4, more than 80% of participants had virologic suppression in TG1–3 when missing data were treated as virologic failure, which was similar to the 84% of participants with virologic suppression in TG4 (Supplementary Fig. 2, http://links.lww.com/QAD/D691).

Mean (standard deviation [SD]) decrease in HIV-1 RNA  \(\log_{10}\)  copies/mL from baseline to Week 80 was 2.96 (0.54) in TG1, 3.08 (0.59) in TG2, 2.96 (0.75) in TG3, and 3.09 (0.76) in TG4. At Week 80, the difference in least squares mean (95% CI) versus TG4 was: 0.08 (-0.19; 0.34;  \(P = .56\) ) for TG1; -0.01 (-0.28; 0.26;  \(P = .96\) ) for TG2; and 0.14 (-0.19; 0.46;  \(P = .40\) ) for TG3. In TG1-3, there was a mean decrease in HIV-1 RNA of approximately 3  \(\log_{10}\)  copies/mL from baseline through Week 132.

Mean (95% CI) increase from baseline in CD4 cell count (cells/μL) was consistent across all groups at Week 80: TG1, 275 (214; 337); TG2, 262 (203; 320); TG3, 245 (174; 315); TG4, 248 (155; 340) (Fig. 3B). No statistical difference was seen between groups at Week 80; difference in least squares mean (95% CI) compared with TG4 was: TG1, 32 (-75; 140;  \(P = .55\) ); TG2, 17 (-80; 115;  \(P = .72\) ); and TG3, -4 (-118; 110;  \(P = .95\) ). At Week 132, mean (95% CI) increase from baseline in CD4 cell count (cells/μL) was: TG1, 265 (200; 329); TG2, 307 (222; 392); TG3, 338 (262; 414) (Fig. 3B).

## Safety

Median (IQR) duration of exposure to any study drug (LEN plus other ARVs for TG1-3 and B/F/TAF for TG4) was 156 (147-172) weeks in TG1, 154 (118-164) weeks in TG2, 141 (103-162) weeks in TG3 and 81 (80-84) weeks in TG4. The number of participants with any-grade TEAEs was generally similar across TGs (Table 1). The most common TEAEs in participants receiving LEN (excluding ISRs) were COVID-19 ( \(n = 30\) ,  \(19\%\) ), influenza ( \(n = 29\) ,  \(18\%\) ), and headache ( \(n = 27\) ,  \(17\%\) ). Grade  \(\geq 3\)  TEAEs occurred in 6 ( \(12\%\) ) participants in TG1, 5 ( \(9\%\) ) participants in TG2, 10 ( \(19\%\) ) participants in TG3, and 2 ( \(8\%\) ) participants in TG4 (Table 1). The only Grade  \(\geq 3\)  TEAE occurring in  \(\geq 1\)  participant was increased blood creatine phosphokinase ( \(n = 4\) ). Serious TEAEs occurred in 4 ( \(8\%\) ) participants in TG1, 4 ( \(8\%\) ) in TG2, and 7 ( \(14\%\) ) in TG3. No serious TEAEs occurred in TG4.

The number of participants who experienced any-grade TEAEs related to study drug was 42 (81%) in TG1, 32 (60%) in TG2, 8 (15%) in TG3, and 4 (16%) in TG4. Two participants experienced Grade 3 TEAEs related to study drug, including injection site abscess (TG1: onset Day 395 and resolution Day 449) and injection site nodules (TG2: onset Day 194 and resolution Day 265). Neither resulted in participant discontinuation from the study. There were no serious TEAEs related to study drug.

Five participants discontinued due to TEAEs. Two participants in TG1 discontinued due to Grade 1 injection site induration  \((n = 1)\)  and Grade 2 viral load increase  \((n = 1)\) . Three participants in TG2 discontinued due to Grade 1 injection site induration  \((n = 2)\) , Grade 1 injection site erythema  \((n = 1)\) , and Grade 1 injection site swelling  \((n = 1)\) ; erythema and swelling occurred in the same participant. Two participants died during the study, one in TG1 (due to non-small cell lung carcinoma) and one in TG3 (cause of death unknown); both deaths were not considered to be related to study drug.

Overall, 103 participants (TG1,  \(n = 51\) ; TG2,  \(n = 52\) ) in the SC LEN total population ( \(n = 105\) ) received at least one injection. Of these, 69 (67%) participants experienced ISRs of any grade. ISR frequency by injection visit was: first, 43%; second, 52%; third, 46%; fourth, 32%; and fifth, 30%. Most common ISRs were erythema (42%), swelling (34%), and pain (28%) (Table 1). ISRs were predominantly Grade 1 or 2, the frequency and severity of the most common ISRs are shown in Fig. 4. Median (IQR) duration of ISRs were short for pain (2 [1-6] days), swelling (10 [5-15] days), and erythema (5 [2-9] days), and longer for nodule (219 [84-372] days) and induration (192 [143-400] days).

Most participants had laboratory abnormalities that were Grade 1 or 2 (Supplementary Table 2, http://links.lww.com/QAD/D691). The number of participants with Grade  \(\geq 3\)  laboratory abnormalities was 16 (31%) in TG1, 20 (38%) in TG2, 23 (44%) in TG3, and 6 (24%) in TG4 (Supplementary Table 3, http://links.lww.com/QAD/D691). Grade 3/4 fasting lipid laboratory abnormalities were infrequent in participants receiving LEN: triglycerides, 4 (3%); hypercholesterolemia, 2 (1%); and high fourth generation low-density lipoproteins, 5 (3%).

### Resistance

No LEN resistance-associated mutations (RAMs) were detected in baseline samples. Of the 182 participants enrolled and dosed, 10 (6%) met virologic failure criteria and were included in the RAP (TG1,  \(n = 3\) ; TG2,  \(n = 2\) ; TG3,  \(n = 4\) ; TG4,  \(n = 1\) ). Four of these participants resuppressed their HIV-1 RNA to <50 copies/mL without a change in regimen or treatment-emergent resistance. Of the six

participants who did not resuppress (TG1,  \(n = 2\) ; TG2,  \(n = 2\) ; TG3,  \(n = 2\) ), two had no treatment-emergent resistance and four developed emergent LEN resistance (TG1,  \(n = 2\) ; TG2,  \(n = 1\) ; TG3,  \(n = 1\) ); three of these occurrences have been previously reported [11, 20]. Further details on participants with emergent LEN resistance can be found in Supplementary Table 4, http://links.lww.com/QAD/D691.

At Week 28, the treatment regimen in TG1 and TG2 was reduced from three ARVs to two. One participant in TG2 developed resistance before Week 28 and three participants in TG1  \((n = 2)\)  and TG3  \((n = 1)\)  developed resistance after Week 28. The participant in TG2 had developed M184M/I RAM in reverse transcriptase prior to Q67H + K70R RAMs in capsid at Week 10; incomplete adherence to F/TAF was suspected [11, 20]. The participant in TG3 developed Q67H RAM in capsid at Week 54 with subsequent emergence of K70R RAM at Week 80 and demonstrated nonadherence to oral LEN by pill count and drug levels. One participant in TG1 developed Q67H + K70R RAMs at Week 80. The other participant in TG1 developed Q67H RAM at Week 116. There was no evidence of adherence issues by drug concentration for either participant in TG1 (Supplementary Table 4, http://links.lww.com/QAD/D691).

# DISCUSSION

Our study demonstrated the long-term virologic efficacy of LEN-containing ARV regimens as initial therapy for PWH. A high proportion of participants had HIV-1 RNA  \(< 50\)  copies/mL in each of the four TGs at Week 80, and virologic suppression remained consistent across all TGs through Week 132. There was a rapid decline in viral load across all TGs that was maintained through Week 132.

Safety data were consistent with the previous Week 54 analysis and no new safety signals emerged [11]. TEAEs leading to discontinuation and Grade  \(\geq 3\)  TEAEs were infrequent, and no serious study drug-related TEAEs were reported. Consistent with previous SC LEN studies [10], ISRs were predominantly mild or moderate and had a short duration (a median of 8 days), apart from nodules and indurations which lasted longer (a median of 31 weeks and 27 weeks, respectively). The frequency of ISRs declined with later injections. Grade  \(3/4\)  fasting lipid laboratory abnormalities were infrequent across TG1-4, consistent with the previous Week 80 analysis where participants receiving LEN experienced expected weight gain and increase in body mass index, consistent with the return to health phenomenon [21].

LEN RAMs (Q67H; Q67H + K70R) were observed in four participants; there was evidence of likely or confirmed nonadherence to oral ARVs in two of these participants, including suspected incomplete adherence to F/TAF in the participant in TG2 and nonadherence to oral LEN by pill count and drug levels in the participant in TG3. In this study, participants received LEN with asynchronously dosed ARVs, which may be associated with the development of resistance. Additional data with synchronously dosed partner agents in PWH will enhance understanding of the resistance barrier of LEN-based regimens in the future.

Treatment-naive studies are essential for evaluating the efficacy of new drugs; this is the first study to evaluate LEN in that context. It was designed to generate exploratory clinical data to assist the future development of LEN-containing regimens and provide supportive safety data for the approval of LEN for HTE PWH, not necessarily to test specific antiretroviral therapy combinations for evaluation in future Phase 3 trials. This study provides insight into the role of LEN as part of a three-drug combination for initial therapy, followed by a two-drug regimen for maintenance. The role of oral and SC LEN in maintenance therapy includes sustaining viral suppression in participants who are already

stable, offering reduced dosing frequency, and potentially simplifying long-term treatment regimens. Due to its long half-life (10–14 days) and potent ARV activity at low doses, oral LEN is being investigated for once-weekly dosing [9]. In an ongoing Phase 2 study (NCT05052996), oral weekly islatravir (ISL) plus LEN maintained high rates of virologic suppression at Week 48 in virologically suppressed PWH [22]. LEN-containing regimens may help provide the resistance profile required to maintain viral suppression in PWH on complex treatment regimens and who are not eligible for other currently available options. Efficacy and safety of switching from a stable complex regimen to once-daily oral bictegravir plus LEN is being investigated in the ongoing, Phase 2/3 ARTISTRY-1 study (NCT05502341) [15]; at Week 48, all 48 participants in the bictegravir  \(75\mathrm{mg} +\)  LEN  \(50\mathrm{mg}\)  group had HIV-1 RNA  \(<50\)  copies/mL [23]. Switching to oral weekly ISL/LEN versus continuing daily B/F/TAF or standard of care in virologically suppressed PWH is also being evaluated in the Phase 3, randomized ISLEND-1 (NCT06630286) and ISLEND-2 (NCT06630299) studies, respectively [16, 17]. Twice-yearly SC LEN has been evaluated for HIV-1 PrEP in the ongoing PURPOSE-1 and PURPOSE-2 studies [13, 14]. Week 52 PURPOSE-1 results demonstrated that twice-yearly SC LEN has  \(100\%\)  efficacy for HIV prevention in cisgender women [13]. In PURPOSE-2, participants receiving twice-yearly SC LEN for 52 weeks had significantly lower HIV incidence than the background incidence and the incidence with daily oral emtricitabine–tenofovir disoproxil fumarate [14].

Our study has several limitations. The sample size for each group was relatively small with a low proportion of women participating. However, it should be noted that there is no LEN pharmacokinetic difference for men versus women [7]. A relatively small proportion of PWH were enrolled with baseline HIV-1 RNA of  \(>100000\)  copies/mL or CD4 counts of  \(<350\)  cells/μL, limiting interpretability of the results in this population with more advanced HIV disease. An additional consideration when interpreting these findings is that discontinuation rates in the study were high; although most discontinuations were not related to efficacy or serious safety concerns, and were likely due to inconvenient study regimens in contrast to a once-daily pill. The long-term safety profile of LEN will continue to be evaluated in ongoing clinical studies.

In conclusion, treatment-naive participants receiving LEN in the CALIBRATE study achieved and maintained a high rate of virologic suppression through Week 132. The safety profile of LEN was consistent with prior analyses, with no new safety signals detected. These longer-term data from CALIBRATE support the further investigation of LEN-based combinations for PWH.

PAPER FULL TEXT # Prevalence of drug resistance mutations and their association with time to virological failure in people living with HIV in Uganda ## Abstract Introduction Despite advancements in antiretroviral therapy (ART), virological failure and drug resistance mutations (DRMs) continue to pose major challenges, especially in resource-limited settings. This study examined DRM prevalence and their association with time to virological failure, informing strategies to optimize HIV treatment outcomes. Methods This cohort study retrospectively reviewed medical records of 235 People living with HIV (PLHIV) who underwent HIV drug resistance testing at the Mildmay-Uganda Hospital from 2018 to 2023. Data on demographics, ART, and DRMs were analyzed. Kaplan-Meier and log-rank tests were used to compare median time to virological failure. Cox proportional hazards models assessed associations factors associated with time to virological failure, with significance set at \(p < 0.05\) . Results Participants had a mean age of 28.0 years, 11.2 years on ART, and DRMs detected in \(59.6\%\) . Mutation prevalence was NNRTIs \((52.8\%)\) , NRTIs \((50.2\%)\) , PI major \((25.5\%)\) , and INSTI \((\leq 0.9\%)\) . Key drug class mutations included, NNRTIs (K103KN \(25.1\%\) , G190AS \(14.0\%\) , Y181CF/V/F \(12.3\%\) ), NRTIs (M184V \(45.0\%\) , T215FY \(30.2\%\) , M41L \(18.3\%\) ), PIs (M46I \(15.7\%\) , V82VA \(12.3\%\) , I54LV \(9.4\%\) ), and INSTIs (E138K, T66A, G118R, E92EV all at \(0.4\%\) ). DRMs were significantly associated with longer time (months) to virological failure: NRTIs (129.3 vs. 88.2, \(p = 0.008\) ), NNRTIs (127.4 vs. 84.2, \(p = 0.003\) ), and PIs (170.9 vs. 88.7, \(p = 0.000\) ). In cox regression analysis, time to virological failure was significantly associated with age (HR: 0.987; CI: 0.976-0.998; \(p = 0.019\) , aHR: 0.976; CI: 0.959-0.993; \(p = 0.007\) ), ART duration (HR: 0.828; CI: 0.800-0.856; \(p = 0.000\) , aHR: 0.827; CI: 0.792-0.863; \(p = 0.000\) ), drug mutations; NRTI (HR: 0.659; CI: 0.484-0.898; \(p = 0.008\) ), NNRTI (HR: 0.628; CI: 0.463-0.851; \(p = 0.003\) ), and PI (HR: 0.257; CI: 0.146-0.453; \(p = 0.000\) , aHR: 0.337; CI: 0.137-0.831; \(p = 0.018\) ). Conclusion Drug resistance is common among PLHIV failing ART, dominated by NNRTI and NRTI mutations. DRMs were present among PLHIV who took a longer time to virological failure. Delayed failure was independently associated with older age, longer ART duration, and PI mutations. Findings support early DRM testing and individualized ART, especially as newer ART options emerge. ## Methods and materials ### Study design This cohort study retrospectively reviewed medical records of People living with HIV-1 who underwent HIV drug resistance testing at the Mildmay Uganda Hospital (MUgH) from 2018 to 2023. ### Study site and population This study was conducted at \(\mathrm{MUgH}\) , a centre of excellence for HIV care and treatment in peri-urban Wakiso District, serving \(\sim 15,000\) PLHIV. Of these, \(65\%\) are female, \(95\%\) are adults aged 18 years and above, and virological suppression stood at \(98\%\) as of 2023 [11]. In line with the HIV programmatic approach, PLHIV on ART who experienced virological failure were requested to undergo HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) testing. The study population comprised participants who had HIV drug resistance tests requested, with results uploaded to the Uganda HIVDR database [12] between 2018 and 2023. We did not identify any participants within this cohort whose results were not included in the HIVDR database. ### Data collection and management Data were collected from April to June 2024, including HIV DRM results, socio-demographic, and medical history from ART registers, patient cards, Electronic Medical Records (EMR), and the National HIVDR database [12]. Data were entered in Excel, exported to Stata, and verified against hard copies. Manual chart reviews addressed EMR gaps [13]. A flowchart illustrates the data collection process. ### Data analysis The analysis was conducted using Stata version 14. Descriptive statistics summarized as frequencies and proportions for categorical variables, means and standard deviations for continuous variables. The most frequent NNRTI mutations were K103KN (25.1%), G190AS (14.0%), and Y181CF/V/F (12.3%). Among NRTI mutations, M184V (45.0%) was the most common, followed by T215FY (30.2%) and M41L (18.3%). Among INSTI major mutations, E138K, T66A, G118R, and E92EV each occurred at 0.4%, with S153SF (0.4%) being the only INSTI accessory mutation detected. ### Time to virological failure versus drug resistance mutations across art regimen drug classes ### Cox proportional hazards analysis of virological failure based on DRMs Table 3 shows that participants with virological failure who were found to have DRMs had a significantly longer median time to virological failure compared to those who had not developed DRMs by the time of virological failure: NRTI (88.2 vs. 129.3 months, \(p = 0.008\) ), NNRTI (84.2 vs. 127.4, \(p = 0.003\) ), PI (88.7 vs. 170.9, \(p = 0.000\) ). ### Survival estimates for drug resistance mutations across ART regimen drug classes Figure 2 below shows Kaplan Meier survival estimates among PLHIV with or without mutations over time. In an estimated period of over 200 months, most PLHIV with mutations at the time of virological failure had exhibited a longer time to virological failure (higher survival time) than those without. However, an exception was observed for INSTI mutations that showed a shorter time to virological failure than in individuals without these mutations. ### Factors associated with time to virological failure Table 4 below summarises the factors associated with time to virological failure in bivariable and multivariable analysis. In the bivariable analysis, factors that showed a significantly longer time to virological failure were age (HR: 0.987; \(95\%\) CI: 0.976-0.998; \(p = 0.019\) ), ART duration (HR: 0.828; \(95\%\) CI: 0.800-0.856; \(p = 0.000\) ), and initiating ART with NNRTI, PI, or NRTI-based regimens \((p < 0.000)\) . Additionally, being underweight (HR: 0.661; \(95\%\) CI: 0.460-0.949; \(p = 0.025\) ), obese (HR: 0.605; \(95\%\) CI: 0.376-0.975; \(p = 0.039\) ) and having NRTI (HR: 0.659; \(95\%\) CI: 0.484-0.898; \(p = 0.008\) ), NNRTI (HR: 0.628; \(95\%\) CI: 0.463-0.851; \(p = 0.003\) ) or PI (HR: 0.257; \(95\%\) CI: 0.146-0.453; \(p = 0.000\) ) mutations as well showed a significantly longer time to virological failure. In multivariable analysis, factors that showed a significantly longer time to virological failure were; age (aHR: 0.976; 95% CI: 0.959-0.993; \(p = 0.007\) ), duration on ART (HR: 0.827; 95% CI: 0.792-0.863; \(p = 0.000\) ), initiation on a PI based regimen (aHR: 0.408; 95% CI: 0.241-0.694; \(p = 0.001\) ) and having PI mutations (aHR: 0.337; 95% CI: 0.137-0.831; \(p = 0.018\) ). ## Discussion This study offers important insights into the role of genotypically guided antiretroviral therapy in enhancing HIV-1treatment outcomes, especially in resource limited settings like Uganda. We evaluated the prevalence of DRMs, and the time taken to virological failure among PLHIV who subsequently presented with DRMs. In this cohort, the mean age was 28 years with an average ART duration of over a decade, which represents a predominantly young population with long-term ART exposure. A slight male predominance was also observed which aligns with national HIV trends in sub-Saharan Africa among PLHIV failing on ART [14]. NRTI-based regimens, particularly AZT- and TDF-based combinations, were the most common initial therapies, reflecting historical treatment guidelines in resource-limited settings [15]. These findings align with previous studies showing widespread use of NNRTI- and NRTI-based regimens, which have been the cornerstone of first-line ART for over two decades [6, 16]. This explains the increased resistance to these regimens, particularly in high HIV burden countries like Uganda. DRM testing for resistance to ART regimens was predominantly done for PLHIV failing on second-line regimens. These regimens Table 3 Cox proportional hazards analysis of median time to virological failure based on DRMs

The study revealed that over half of the participants harboured DRMs, with NNRTI and NRTI mutations emerging as the most prevalent. This finding is consistent with earlier research highlighting the low genetic barrier of NNRTIs and the historical reliance on thymidine analogues like AZT, which are linked to characteristic resistance mutations [17].
