observed, though less frequent than NNRTI and NRTI mutations. This is likely due to the higher genetic barrier of protease inhibitors and their more restricted use in second- and third-line ART [8, 10]. Major and accessory INSTI mutations were rare \((< 1\%)\) , reflecting limited exposure to this drug class. Nevertheless, their presence, even at low levels, raises concern given the increasing global use of dolutegravir as a first line anchor drug [15]. This study provided a detailed characterization of the prevalence of specific DRMs across major ART drug classes: PIs, INSTIs, NRTIs, and NNRTIs. Among NNRTI mutations, K103N/S/KN were the most prevalent. This mutation is particularly concerning as it confers high-level resistance to first-line NNRTIs such as nevirapine and efavirenz, limiting HIV treatment options. The dominance of K103N/S/KN in this cohort is consistent with previous studies indicating a high prevalence of NNRTI resistance, which exceeds the WHO resistance threshold and emphasises the need for alternative regimens, such as those incorporating INSTIs or PIs [10, 19, 20]. In the NRTI category, M184V/MV/MIV was most prevalent, highlighting the widespread resistance to lamivudine and emtricitabine, which are present in almost all ART regimens prescribed in Uganda. This mutation not only reduces the effectiveness of these drugs but paradoxically increases susceptibility to other NRTIs, like TDF and AZT, potentially allowing for continued viral suppression when used in combination with other drugs [21, 22]. However, the high prevalence of this mutation in the study emphasizes the need for caution when prescribing regimens containing these NRTIs. Among PI mutations, M46I, I54LV, and V82VA were the most common, conferring high level resistance to protease inhibitors like atazanavir and lopinavir and low level resistance to darunavir, which are often used in second and third line ART regimens [18, 23]. The high prevalence of these mutations suggests that the efficacy of PI-based second line and to lesser extent third line treatment may be compromised. This stresses the need for careful monitoring and consideration of alternative options for patients experiencing treatment failure. In contrast, INSTI mutations were found at a much lower prevalence, likely reflecting the recent introduction of INSTIs such as dolutegravir (DTG) in ART regimens. The major INSTI mutations that occurred were; T66A, G118R, and E138K which could potentially affect the efficacy of INSTIs, particularly in cases of virological failure consistent with findings from a study done Mozambique [24]. The analysis of time to virological failure demonstrated a statistically significant association with the subsequent emergence of DRMs. PLHIV who developed DRMs experienced a longer median time to virological failure, possibly reflecting better adherence in this group. Previous studies from low- and middle income countries report that the median time to first-line ART failure ranges from 50 days to over 31 months, depending on factors such as ART regimen, adherence, baseline CD4 count, and prior ART exposure [25, 26]. While many PLHIV experience early treatment failure, prolonged viral suppression allows for the gradual accumulation of drug resistance mutations (DRMs). Our findings suggest that by 10 years on ART, PLHIV are likely to develop DRMs and subsequent virological failure, supporting our recommendation that individuals with a decade of ART undergo resistance testing to enable early detection of DRMs and timely optimization of therapy. These findings further suggest that DRMs tend to emerge after extended ART use, highlighting the potential of time to virological failure as a predictor for the occurrence of DRMs and a tool for informing optimized treatment planning. Also, a longer time to virological failure may reflect sustained ART effectiveness despite the presence of emerging mutations, a situation further influenced by the practice of aligning HIV drug resistance testing with confirmed virological failure. Therefore, the occurrence of resistance mutations may as well be linked to delayed DRMs detection rather than sole influence of a longer time to virological failure. Enhanced care strategies such as enhanced adherence counselling may as well contribute to delayed virological failure [27]. Additionally, non-canonical mutations outside traditional drug target regions may restore viral fitness or modulate drug susceptibility, potentially delaying treatment failure [28]. The predominant presence of M184V mutations, which have been cited to reduce viral fitness and delay virological failure augment the explanation. This mutation not only confers resistance to specific drugs but also increases susceptibility to other NRTIs like TDF and AZT, supporting the delayed failure phenomenon [21, 22]. It is also important to note that, prior to the implementation of current HIV treatment guidelines, limited access to genotypic testing likely delayed the timely detection of DRMs [7]. The INSTI mutations did not yield statistically significant results for time to virological failure analysis possibly due to the small sample size of INSTI-treated PLHIV. Overall, these findings emphasize the importance of regular genotype testing, especially for patients with persistent non-suppressed viral loads despite adherence efforts and support the implementation of personalized ART regimens to optimize treatment outcomes [9, 24]. The analysis of factors associated with virological failure demonstrated that age and ART duration were protective against virological failure. Older individuals and those on ART for longer duration experienced significantly reduced hazards for shorter time to virological failure. This likely reflects the benefits of sustained treatment and adherence, as long-term ART users often adapt their lifestyles for viral suppression and may experience fewer side effects, reducing the risk of discontinuation [29]. Older patients may also benefit from stronger support systems and greater ART literacy, contributing to better outcomes [30]. These findings contrast with a meta-analysis linking prolonged ART duration to higher failure risk [31], suggesting variability across contexts. Younger individuals, often facing stigma, limited support, and behavioural challenges, and were more vulnerable to failure [30]. These findings highlight the importance of age-related considerations in managing HIV treatment and suggest that younger individuals may benefit from tailored interventions that address the unique barriers they face. Having an underweight or obese BMI were associated with a reduced hazard of virological failure. However, this finding was not significant in the multivariable model indicating high influence of confounders. Non the less, this may be partly explained by the metabolic effects of certain ART regimens, some of which are linked to muscle wasting regardless of their virological effectiveness, while others are associated with weight gain. These complex dynamics are better explained by studies with pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic models to explain causality. Contrary, some studies have reported wasting as a marker of advanced HIV disease and virological failure [32], suggesting that further research with detailed pharmacological and clinical assessments is needed to fully understand this phenomenon [33]. ### Limitations While this study provides important insights, several limitations warrant caution. First, the relatively small sample size, particularly for patients with INSTI mutations, may limit the generalizability of the findings. In addition, potential confounders such as genetic variation, HIV clade, contextual factors including treatment interruptions, and possible selection bias may have influenced the observed associations. The study's retrospective, observational design restricts its ability to establish clear cause-and-effect relationships, partly because some important variables needed to assess causality were missing. Larger, prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings. However, this study benefits from real-world, clinic-based data, capturing PLHIV who were clinically diagnosed with ART failure offering contextually relevant insights into treatment dynamics. Moreover, the population characteristics in this cohort reflect expected patterns in similar high-risk groups, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where access to HIV resistance testing remains limited. ## Conclusion Drug resistance remains a substantial challenge among PLHIV failing on ART, with NNRTI and NRTI mutations dominating the resistance landscape. While DRMs were present among PLHIV who took a longer time of virological failure, the findings emphasize the need for early DRM testing, individualized treatment strategies and proactive regimen switching. The study further emphasises significant role of patient-specific factors, such as age and ART duration, in influencing time to virological failure. Future studies should explore longitudinal outcomes with newer agents, including long-acting injectables and second-generation INSTIs, to inform the next phase of ART optimization in high-burden settings. These findings carry several programmatic implications. First, the high prevalence of DRMs, highlights the importance of routine viral load monitoring and timely DRM testing to guide treatment modifications. Second, the potential for paradoxical protective effects of certain mutations invites further investigation into functional resistance, viral fitness, and regimen interactions. Lastly, as integrase inhibitors become more widely used, robust surveillance is needed to monitor emerging resistance, especially in resource-limited settings where second- and third-line options remain constrained. ### Data availability The data sets for this study are available upon reasonable request from the corresponding author. PAPER ENDED

**Study Objectives**
The objective of this project is to systematically extract and curate data related to HIV drug resistance from published reports. For each paper, identify and summarize information on:

1. HIV nucleotide or amino-acid sequences obtained from clinical samples, including GenBank accession numbers.
2. The populations from whom HIV sequences were obtained.
3. The clinical samples and sequencing methods used.
4. Antiretroviral \(ARV\) treatment histories of the individuals whose samples were sequenced.

**Question 1 – Does the paper report HIV sequences from patient samples?**
**Goal:** Determine whether the study generated new HIV nucleotide or amino-acid sequences, or reported lists of mutations, directly from clinical samples obtained from individuals with HIV \(ART-naïve or ART-experienced\).
**Answer “Yes” if the paper:**

- States that genetic sequencing, genotypic resistance testing, Sanger sequencing, next-generation sequencing, or single-genome sequencing was performed on clinical samples such as plasma, serum, PBMCs, proviral DNA, or dried blood spots.
- Indicates that sequencing was done on samples from patients, participants, subjects, blood donors, newly diagnosed or newly infected individuals, PLWH/PWH, or cohorts of individuals with HIV.
- States that surveillance for transmitted or acquired drug resistance was performed and generated new sequence data.
- Reports GenBank accession numbers for sequences generated in the study.

**Answer “No” if:**

- Only laboratory strains \(e.g., HXB2, IIIB, NL4-3, BAL, LAI\) or site-directed mutants were studied.
- The paper is a review or meta-analysis using sequences reported in other studies or downloaded from databases without generating new sequences.

**Question 2 – Does the paper report in vitro drug susceptibility data?**
**Goal:** Determine whether the paper quantifies HIV in vitro susceptibility to ARV drugs.
**Answer “Yes” if the paper:**

- States that phenotypic susceptibility testing, phenotypic resistance testing, or a drug susceptibility assay was performed.
- Reports IC₅₀, EC₅₀, EC₉₀, fold change in susceptibility, or similar measures.
- Describes a susceptibility assay \(e.g., PhenoSense/Monogram, Antivirogram/Virco\) or gives details on cells, drug titrations, and reporter readouts.
- Specifies the virus used for testing \(e.g., clinical isolate, site-directed mutant, virus from in vitro passage\).

Otherwise, answer “No”.

**Question 3 – Were sequences from the paper made publicly available?**
**Goal:** Determine whether newly generated HIV sequences or raw reads were deposited in public repositories \(e.g., GenBank, SRA, DDBJ, ENA\).
**Answer “Yes” if the paper:**

- Provides GenBank accession numbers \(typically two letters followed by digits\) in the Methods, Results, a Supplementary Table, or Data Availability statement.
- States that sequences have been submitted to GenBank or another public database, even if accession numbers are “pending.”
- States that raw reads are available in SRA or other sequence-read repositories.

**Answer “No” if:**

- Only accession numbers for HIV reference strains \(e.g., HXB2, NL4-3, LAI, BAL\) are given.
- No accession numbers or deposition statements are provided.
- Only accession numbers from previous studies are cited.
- The paper is a review or meta-analysis using existing sequence data.

**Question 4 – What are the GenBank accession numbers for sequenced HIV isolates?**

- If the paper reports that sequences were submitted to GenBank or another public database and provides accession numbers, extract all individual accession numbers and ranges \(e.g., FJ800379–FJ800386; GQ477441–GQ477451; KP170487\).
- Accession numbers may appear in the Methods, in a table, in Supplementary material, or in a Data Availability statement.
- If accession numbers are described but extraction is ambiguous, copy the relevant text describing the submission.

If no accession numbers are given, answer “Not reported”.

**Question 5 – How many individuals had samples obtained for HIV sequencing?**

- If the paper does **not** report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, or only compiles sequences from databases/previous studies, answer **0**.
- If sequencing or genotypic resistance testing was performed on samples or sequences from X individuals, answer **X**.
- If the paper reports X isolates/sequences from a group of patients but does not specify how many individuals contributed isolates, assume one sequence per individual and answer **X**, unless stated otherwise.
- If multiple mutually exclusive patient groups are described, sum individuals across all groups.
- If sequences were generated but the number of individuals is not reported, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 6 – From which countries were the sequenced samples obtained?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, answer **“Not applicable”**.
- Use the country or countries where samples were collected \(e.g., recruitment, enrollment, follow-up, or surveillance site\).
- If multiple countries are listed, report all.
- If samples were collected in country A and sequenced in country B, report **country A**.
- If no country information is provided, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 7 – From what years were the sequenced samples obtained?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, answer **“Not applicable”**.
- If sample collection dates are reported \(e.g., Year1–Year2, or month/year ranges\), report the year span \(e.g., “June 2004–April 2007” → **2004–2007**\).
- If samples are listed by individual years \(e.g., 2008, 2009, 2010\), report the full span \(e.g., **2008–2010**\).
- If only months within a single year are reported \(e.g., March–September 2008\), report that single year \(**2008**\).
- If baseline sequencing corresponds to enrollment or diagnosis years, use that year range.
- If no sample-collection years are provided, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 8 – Were samples cloned prior to sequencing?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV **or** does not report in vitro susceptibility data, answer **“Not applicable”**.
- Answer **“Yes”** if:
    - The paper states that “amplicons were cloned and sequenced,” or describes use of a cloning method \(e.g., TA/Topo TA cloning\).
    - Molecular clones were sequenced.
    - Single-genome amplification or limiting dilution was performed prior to sequencing.
    - Site-directed mutagenesis was performed on isolates that were sequenced.
- Answer **“No”** if:
    - Direct PCR or population-based sequencing is reported.
    - A commercial genotyping platform \(e.g., ViroSeq, TruGene, GeneSeqR, GenoSure, Vela Diagnostics\) is used.
    - Next-generation sequencing \(NGS\) without cloning is used.
- If cloning information is not provided, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 9 – Which HIV genes were reported to have been sequenced?**
Report all applicable gene targets using the abbreviations **PR**, **RT**, **IN**, **Pol**, **CA** \(capsid\), and **Env**.

- If the paper states “pol genotyping/sequencing” without further detail, answer **“Pol”**.
- If “protease and reverse transcriptase,” “PR/RT,” “ViroSeq,” or “TruGene \(PR/RT\)” are mentioned, include **PR** and **RT**.
- If “integrase,” “IN,” “GeneSeq/ViroSeq Integrase,” “INSTI resistance,” or “integrase sequencing” are mentioned, include **IN**.
- If NRTI or NNRTI resistance is assessed, include **RT**.
- If PI resistance is assessed, include **PR**.
- If INSTI resistance is assessed, include **IN**.
- If lenacapavir resistance is assessed, include **CA** \(capsid\).
- If “env,” “gp120,” “gp41,” “gp160,” “V3 loop/C2V3,” or coreceptor-usage genotyping is reported, include **Env**.

**Question 10 – What method was used for sequencing?**

- Answer **“Sanger sequencing”** if:
    - Dideoxy \(dideoxyterminator\) or Sanger sequencing is explicitly mentioned.
    - ABI or Thermo Fisher sequencing reagents/instruments are used.
    - Capillary electrophoresis, electropherograms, or “direct PCR sequencing” are described.
    - The paper was published before 2008 \(NGS was not widely used\).
- Answer **“NGS”** if:
    - “Next-generation sequencing,” “NGS,” or “ultra-deep sequencing” is reported.
    - Illumina platforms \(MiSeq, HiSeq, iSeq\), Oxford Nanopore \(e.g., GridION\), PacBio RSII/SMRT, 454 pyrosequencing, Sentosa, or Vela NGS systems are used.
- If the sequencing method is not described, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 11 – What type of samples were sequenced?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, answer **“Not applicable”**.
- If viral RNA was extracted from plasma or serum, include **“Plasma”**.
- If samples were obtained at diagnosis or at virological failure, they are likely plasma: include **“Plasma”**.
- If PBMCs, peripheral blood mononuclear cells, or proviral DNA are mentioned, include **“PBMC”**.
- If samples were from individuals with stable virological suppression, they are often PBMCs: include **“PBMC”**.
- If nucleic acids were extracted from whole blood, include **“Whole blood”**.
- If dried blood spots are used, include **“DBS”**.
- If other sample types \(e.g., lymph node, cerebrospinal fluid\) are used, list those specifically.
- If the specimen type for sequencing is not stated, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 12 – Were any sequences obtained from individuals with virological failure on a treatment regimen?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, answer **“Not applicable”**.
- Answer **“Yes”** if:
    - Samples were from patients with virological failure or virological rebound.
    - Sequencing was performed on plasma from ART-experienced individuals.
    - Samples were obtained from patients on second-line treatment.
    - Patients had received NRTIs, NNRTIs, PIs, and/or INSTIs and sequences were generated.
- Answer **“No”** if:
    - All sequenced patients were newly diagnosed or ART-naïve.
    - Sequencing was done exclusively for transmitted drug-resistance surveillance \(i.e., untreated individuals\).

**Question 13 – Were the patients in the study in a clinical trial?**

- Answer **“Yes”** if the paper:
    - Describes randomization to different treatments.
    - Describes a study as double-blind, placebo-controlled, open-label, controlled, or multicenter.
    - Describes a phase 1, 2, or 3 trial.
- Answer **“No”** if the paper:
    - Describes an observational or prospective cohort, retrospective or cross-sectional study, case-control study, or case series.
    - Provides no information suggesting clinical-trial participation.

**Note:** Registration at ClinicalTrials.gov \(NCT number\) alone is not sufficient to classify a study as a clinical trial.

**Question 14 – Does the paper report HIV sequences from individuals who had previously received ARV drugs?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, answer **“No”**.
- Answer **“Yes”** if sequences were obtained from individuals who:
    - Were receiving ART, were ART-experienced or treatment-experienced, or had virological failure/rebound.
    - Were receiving specific ARV classes \(NRTIs, NNRTIs, PIs, INSTIs, capsid inhibitors, entry inhibitors\) or specific drugs \(e.g., 3TC, FTC, AZT, TDF, abacavir, efavirenz, rilpivirine, doravirine, atazanavir, lopinavir, darunavir, raltegravir, elvitegravir, dolutegravir, bictegravir, cabotegravir, lenacapavir, maraviroc, fostemsavir, enfuvirtide, ibalizumab\).
    - Had stable virological suppression on ART.
    - Acquired HIV infection while receiving PrEP.
    - Include both ART-naïve and ART-experienced individuals \(any history of ARV use → “Yes”\).
- Answer **“No”** if **all** sequences were from ART-naïve, treatment-naïve, drug-naïve, previously unexposed, or newly diagnosed individuals, or from individuals in a pure transmitted drug-resistance surveillance study.

**Question 15 – Which drug classes were received by individuals in the study before sample sequencing?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, answer **“None”**.
- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals who had previously received ARVs, answer **“None”**.

Otherwise, list all applicable drug classes:

- If the paper names drug classes directly \(NRTIs, NNRTIs, PIs, INSTIs, capsid inhibitors, entry inhibitors\), list those.
- If only specific drugs are named, infer classes:
    - **NRTIs:** zidovudine/AZT, lamivudine/3TC, emtricitabine/FTC, tenofovir \(TDF/TAF\), abacavir/ABC, stavudine/d4T, didanosine/ddI.
    - **NNRTIs:** efavirenz/EFV, nevirapine/NVP, etravirine/ETR, rilpivirine/RPV, doravirine/DOR.
    - **PIs:** lopinavir/r \(LPV/r\), atazanavir/ATV, darunavir/DRV, saquinavir/SQV, indinavir/IDV, nelfinavir/NFV, tipranavir/TPV, fosamprenavir/FPV.
    - **INSTIs:** raltegravir/RAL, elvitegravir/EVG, dolutegravir/DTG, bictegravir/BIC, cabotegravir/CAB.
    - **Capsid inhibitors \(CAIs\):** lenacapavir/LEN.
    - **Entry inhibitors:** maraviroc/MVC, fostemsavir, enfuvirtide, ibalizumab.

Additional rules:

- If all sequences are from ART-naïve/treatment-naïve/drug-naïve individuals, answer **“None”**.
- If a pre-2020 paper states that individuals were receiving a first-line WHO regimen, include **NRTI** and **NNRTI**.
- If a pre-2020 paper states that individuals were receiving a second-line WHO regimen, include **NRTI**, **NNRTI**, and **PI**.
- If individuals are described only as “ART-experienced” without drugs or classes, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 16 – Which drugs were received by individuals in the study before sample sequencing?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, answer **“None”**.
- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals who had previously received ARVs, answer **“None”**.
- If sequences were obtained from ART-experienced individuals but no specific drugs are named, answer **“Not reported”**.
- If only drug classes \(e.g., NRTIs, NNRTIs, PIs, INSTIs\) are mentioned without individual drugs, answer **“Not reported”**.

# Molecular characterization of a unique Recombinant form of HIV-1 subtype F2/ CRF02_AG identified in Guangdong, China


## Abstract

Background The human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) pandemic continues to pose a significant global public health challenge. Recombination between HIV-1 variants generates unique recombinant forms (URFs) and then circulating recombinant forms (CRFs) after ongoing transmission. Subtype F2 and CRF02_AG mainly spread in western Africa, but they are rarely detected in China. Here, we observed a URF composed of subtypes F2 and CRF02_AG isolated from a man (230794) in Guangdong, China.

Methods The near full-length genome (NFLG) of HIV-1 was amplified with two overlapping segments by the near endpoint dilution method. The positive products were sequenced directly to obtain genomic sequences. The recombinant pattern and breakpoints of the NFLG were determined using the Simplot software and confirmed by maximum likelihood (ML) trees for segments using the IQtree tool. The maximum clade credibility (MCC) tree was reconstructed to trace the origin by using BEAST software. Genotypic drug resistance data were interpreted by the Stanford HIV Drug Resistance Database. The co-receptor tropism was predicted using the geno2pheno coreceptor 2.5 tool, the WebPSSM tool and the HIVcoPRED tool.

Results The individual (230794) was 47 years old and got infected via heterosexual contact in Guangzhou City, Guangdong Province. The NFLG sequence of strain 230794 was 8260 nucleotides (nt) in length, with two CRF02_AG segments substituting in the backbone of subtype F2 in the vif and env gene regions. The genomic recombinant mosaic structures of 230794 were different from those of the other nine issued subtype F2/CRF02_AG URFs. No drug-resistant mutation was identified, but an INSTI other mutation, L74l, was identified. Strain 230794 was predicted to be a X4/R5 dual-tropism strain. Bayesian inference indicated that strain 230794 originated approximately between 2015 and 2018.

Conclusion A novel URF of subtype F2/CRF02_AG was identified from a Cantonese man, with R5/X4 dual tropism. It is necessary to strengthen the molecular surveillance of the spread of recombinant strains in regions with high HIV-1 genetic diversity in China.


### Methods

#### Ethical issues

This study was approved by the institutional review board of Guangzhou Eighth People's Hospital (No. 202353290), and the individual provided written informed consent.

#### Source of the specimen

In the previous drug resistance surveillance among 5602 HIV-1-infected antiretroviral therapy (ART)-naive individuals in Guangdong Province from Jan. 2023 to Dec. 2023, we identified one partial pol gene sequence in a plasma specimen collected from an HIV-1-infected patient, 230794, as a suspected recombinant of subtype F2 and CRF02_AG, two subtypes of HIV that are very rare in China and even worldwide. Specimen 230794 was collected in Oct. 2023 from a 47-year-old man who claimed to have contracted HIV-1 through heterosexual contact in Guangzhou City, Guangdong Province, China. His spouse was negative for HIV-1. The baseline HIV-1 viral load was  \(3.95 \times 10^5\)  IU/mL, and the  \(\mathrm{CD4^{+}}\)  T-cell count was 77 cells/μL. These values indicated that this patient was in the advanced stage of HIV-1 infection, which had not been identified and treated in a timely manner, resulting in severe immune system damage.

#### Nucleic acid extraction, amplification, sequencing, and sequence assembly

Viral RNA was extracted from the 2023 plasma sample using a magnetic bead-based method. RNA was reverse transcribed to cDNA using the SuperScript III System. Proviral DNA was extracted from the whole-blood sample collected in 2025 with the Viral DNA Extraction Kit (Supbio, China). Two overlapping halves of the HIV-1 genome were subsequently amplified by nested polymerase chain reaction (PCR) by utilizing LA Taq (TaKaRa, China) with a near endpoint dilution method as described previously [19]. Positive products were directly purified and sequenced by Sangon Biotech (Shanghai) Co., Ltd with Sanger sequencing method. The NFLG was assembled and cleaned by the software Sequencher

V5.1 (Gene Codes, United States). The obtained NFLG sequence was examined with the Quality Control Tool in the HIV database (https://www.hiv.lanl.gov/content/sequence/QC/index.html) to check for potential contamination and confirm sequence quality thereby excluding the occurrence of stop codons, frameshifts, non-ACGT characters, hypermutations, and other such issues.

#### Phylogenetic and recombination breakpoints analysis of sequences

The neighbor-joining (NJ) phylogenetic tree of the NFLG was constructed using the Kimura 2-parameter model with 1000 bootstrap replications in Mega software V11.0.11 with reference sequences downloaded from the Los Alamos HIV database (https://www.hiv.lanl.gov/content/index), including 10 subtypes (A-D, F-H, and J-L), CRF01_AE, CRF02_AG, CRF07_BC, and group N.

A preliminary analysis of recombination patterns was conducted using the online tools of the LANL HIV sequence database, including jumping profile Hidden Markov Model (jpHMM) [20] and Recombinant Identification Program (RIP) with a window size of 400 bp. Similarity and BootScan analyses were performed by using SimPlot software V3.5 to further investigate the characteristics of the recombinant form.

Subregion maximum likelihood (ML) phylogenetic trees were constructed with the appropriate addition of parental subtype sequences as references to validate the recombinant form. The ML phylogenetic trees were constructed by using the general time reversible (GTR) substitution model with 1000 ultrafast bootstrap replications to assess the reliability of the internal branches with IQtree [21] (https://www.hiv.lanl.gov/content/sequence/IQTREE/qttree.html).

The recombination pattern diagram was drawn with the Recombinant HIV-1 Drawing Tool [22] in the Los Alamos HIV Sequence Database (https://www.hiv.lanl.gov/content/sequence/DRAW_CRF/recom Mapper.html) according to the corresponding positions of the international standard strain HXB2.

#### Analysis of the source of parental strains

To estimate the origin of strain 230794, Bayesian molecular clock analyses were performed. The quasispecies sequences obtained from plasma and whole-blood samples collected at different time points were used to explore the times of most recent common ancestors (tMRCAs) using the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) inference implemented in BEAST software V1.10 [23]. The MCMC evolutionary analyses were performed for  \(2 \times 10^{\wedge}8\)  steps with sampling every 5000 steps under the GTR nucleotide substitution model, the uncorrelated relaxed clock model, and the Bayesian skyline prior mode. The subtype F2 and CRF02_AG sequences

worldwide were downloaded from the HIV database and selected to reconstruct the topology of the maximum clade credibility (MCC) tree. The convergence of parameters was checked using Tracer v1.7.1 and the effective sample size (ESS) value was  \(>200\) . The initial  \(10\%\)  of the states of each run were burn-in using TreeAnnotator 1.10.4. The MCC trees were visualized and edited in FigTree 1.4.0 [24].

#### Drug resistance and genotypic co-receptor analysis

The HIVdb program from the Stanford HIV Drug Resistance Database (https://hivdb.stanford.edu/hivdb/by-sequences/) was used to analyse the protease inhibitors (PIs), nucleoside reverse-transcription inhibitors (NRTIs), non-nucleoside reverse-transcription inhibitors (NNRTIs), integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) and drug resistance mutations (DRMs). The V3-loop sequence of the NFLG was obtained using the GeneCutter tool. The co-receptor tropism was predicted using the geno2pheno coreceptor 2.5 tool (http://coreceptor.geno2pheno.org/) with a  \(5\%\)  false-positive rate (FPR) th reshold (recommended for CRF02_AG strains) [25], the WebPSSM[x4r5] tool (https://indra.mullins.microbiol.w ashington.edu/webpssm/) [26] and the HIVcoPRED tool (https://webs.iitd.edu.in/raghava/hivcopred/submit.htm l) [27].

## Results

### Common characteristics and phylogenetic analysis of the NFLG sequence

The NFLG sequence of 230794, which was 8260 nucleotides (nt) in length, was obtained and submitted to GenBank (accession number PV187006).

In the NJ phylogenetic tree reconstructed with full-length genome sequences, strain 230794 formed a distinct branch within the subtype F clade (bootstrap value  \(= 100\%\) ), as illustrated in Fig. 1A. Phylogenetic analysis revealed a close topological relationship among strain 230794, subtype F1 and subtype F2, indicating that strain 230794 likely represents a novel recombinant variant. After submitting the NFLG sequence to the HIV BLAST tool in the HIV database (https://www.hiv.lanl.gov/content/sequence/BASIC_BLAST/basic_blast.html), the two most similar sequences to 230794, MK086126, and MK086128 were both subtype F2/CRF02_AG recombinant strains with identities of  \(87\%\) , indicating that 230794 might be a subtype F2/CRF02_AG recombinant virus.

### Prediction of drug resistance mutations and tropism

No major/accessory mutations conferring resistance to PIs, NRTIs, NNRTIs, or INSTIs were identified, therefore, the strain 230794 was susceptible to 26 drugs in four categories (as shown in Supplementary Table 2). However, the strain 230794 harbors an INSTI other mutation, L74I, which is highly polymorphic and is not more common in individuals receiving INSTIs than in INSTI-naive individuals [28]. The V3 loop amino acid sequence was identified as "CTRPGNNTRKGVHIGPGRAFYTM-DITGDIRQAFC". Genotypic co-receptor analysis using Geno2pheno (5% FPR threshold) and the WebPSSM tool predicted exclusive CCR5 tropism, whereas the HIV-coPRED tool predicted CXCR4 usage. Considering the reported low sensitivity of V3 sequence-based prediction tools for non-B subtypes [29], genotypic tools alone may not reliably exclude CXCR4 variants, therefore, strain 230794 was classified as a potentially X4/R5 dual-tropic strain.

## Discussion

Subtype F2 and CRF02_AG are prevalent mainly in western Africa but are rarely detected in China. CRFs consisting of subtype F2 and CRF02_AG have not yet emerged. In this study, we identified a URF composed of subtypes F2 and CRF02_AG from a specimen isolated in Guangdong Province. Analysis of the genomic recombinant mosaic structures revealed that the breakpoints of strain 230794 and the other nine reported recombinants of subtype F2/CRF02_AG were various (Fig. 3). In the gag gene region, nine of the recombinants consisted of the pure subtype F2 or pure CRF02_AG, and only one of them (MK086112) contained components of subtype F2 and CRF02_AG. In the pol gene region, nine of the strains presented different breakpoint locations, with insertions of the CRF02_AG fragment (MK086112, MK086120, MK086126, and PV187006) or insertions of the subtype F2 fragment (KR017771, MK086115, and MK086117-119). In addition, three of the strains had insertions at the initial position of the pol region and six of them had insertions at the C-terminus of the pol region. In the env gene region, only one strain (MK086126) had breakpoints with insertions of CRF02_AG fragments into the subtype F2 backbone. These findings indicate that conventional pol gene drug resistance surveillance may be helpful in identifying subtype F2/CRF02_AG recombinant strains.

A West African study revealed a high proportion of L74I in CRF02_AG [32]. Whether L74I in CRF02_AG affects INSTI resistance can be confirmed through additional in vitro resistance experiments. For patient 230794, in Jan 2024 (three months after ART), the HIV-1 RNA viral load test result was  \(369~\mathrm{IU / mL}\) . In Apr 2024, Oct 2024 and Apr 2025, the patient got successful suppression, with the HIV-1 RNA viral load below the detection limit. These findings suggested that the presence of the mutation L74I may not affect the efficacy of b拮egravir, emtricitabine and tenofovir alafenamide (BIC + FTC + TAF) combination treatment.

In a previous study of a large cohort of antiretroviral-naive individuals in Canada, it was shown that participants with R5/X4 HIV-1 had the poorest clinical profiles, with the highest plasma viral loads, and the lowest CD4 cell counts and were more likely to develop acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)-defining illness before therapy initiation than participants harboring only R5-tropic HIV-1 strains [33]. The baseline  \(\mathrm{CD4^{+}}\)  T-cell count of patient 230794 was critically low at 77 cells/  \(\mu \mathrm{L}\) , which is consistent with the clinical profile of R5/

X4 HIV-1 infection. Following ART initiation, the  \(\mathrm{CD4^{+}}\)  T-cell counts gradually increased, reaching 192, 148, 203, 230, 253 and 191 cells/  \(\mu \mathrm{L}\)  at 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18 months post-ART, respectively. While the observed  \(\mathrm{CD4^{+}}\)  T-cell count recovery indicates the therapeutic efficacy of ART, the decelerated progression after the initial 6 months suggests potential constraints in immune reconstitution. This suboptimal recovery underscores the detrimental impact of R5/X4 HIV-1, particularly the CXCR4-tropic variants, which may exacerbate chronic immune activation, suppress naive T-cell production and promote apoptosis [34].

According to national treatment strategies in China, the HIV patients on ART should be followed up to evaluate the ART efficacy. The patient 230794 obtained successful viral suppression with plasma viral load below the detection limit in 2025, therefore, we chose to harvest viral DNA from the whole blood sample. By comparing the genetic sequences obtained in 2023 and 2025, it was found that they were largely genetically similar, without obvious difference in the recombination forms. On the basis of time-scaled phylogenetic analyses, the tMRCAs of the subtype F2 and CRF02_AG segments were estimated at 2018.87 and 2015.05, respectively. This temporal overlap suggests that HIV-1 strain 230794 likely

emerged during the 2015-2018 period through recombination events between these circulating lineages. Analysis of the ML tree reconstructed using the partial pol gene region of HIV-1 strain 230794 and all 127 subtype F2 reference sequences downloaded from the HIV sequence database (coordinate to HXB2 2253-3272) revealed evolutionary clustering between the subtype F2 parental lineage of HIV-1 strain 230794 and two Canadian-derived sequences (bootstrap value = 100%, Supplementary Fig. 1). In the 2000s, armed conflicts in Africa led to an influx of newcomers from HIV-endemic areas (including Cameroon, Congo and Rwanda) into Canada [35], which may explain the introduction of non-clade B viruses into Canada. Therefore, the subtype F2 parental lineage of HIV-1 strain 230794 might have originated from Africa. According to the ML tree reconstructed using the partial env gene region of HIV-1 strain 230794 and 283 globally representative CRF02_AG reference sequences downloaded from the HIV sequence database (coordinate to HXB2 6420-8384), the CRF02_AG parental lineage of the HIV-1 strain 230794 monophyletic clade (bootstrap value = 100%) completely segregated from all Chinese sequences and showed no significant clustering with any other CRF02_AG reference sequences (Supplementary Fig. 2), suggesting non-Chinese origins for the CRF02_AG progenitor of this recombinant strain. According to the in-depth epidemiological investigation, patient 230794 claimed that he had never been abroad. He self-reported having several heterosexual sexual partners, but in the following tracking, we failed to locate his former partners and confirm their HIV-1 status. Therefore, we speculated that HIV-1 strain 230794 may be a recombinant strain from abroad rather than a local strain prevalent in Guangdong, China.

In light of the molecular prevalence of subtypes F2 and CRF02_AG in Guangdong and their predominance in foreign countries, the strain was most likely introduced into China through travel or prosperous trade between Guangdong and foreign countries. HIV-1 genetic diversity poses major challenges to many aspects, including HIV vaccine development pathogenicity, ART efficacy, drug resistance, and diagnostic assays [4]. The current spouse of patient 230794 tested negative for HIV-1 antibodies, and no related recombinant strains were detected in our conventional pol gene drug resistance surveillance after 2023. Although the imported subtype F2/CRF02_AG recombinant strain may not have spread further, continuous follow-up of this case is necessary. Moreover, testing services and molecular surveillance should be performed for migrants or foreign travelers, and effective interventions can be tailored to infections to prevent the potential spread of new HIV variants.

Our study has certain limitations. Firstly, the fragment  \((3144\pm 90\mathrm{nt})\)  did not get further phylogenetic analysis,

for its too short (only 180 nucleotides) in length with low sequence similarity, ambiguous signals or complex recombination scenarios. This may lead to deviations in breakpoint determination, hard to judge recombination patterns and track the possible parental strains. Secondly, the pol gene was routinely amplified and harvested for drug resistance surveillance before the initial ART in China. It may miss a proportion of recombinant strains, since genetic recombination can occur throughout the HIV-1 genome, and more evidence support the recombination events involving regions outside of pol, such as env or gag. Thirdly, we only got 4 or 3 single genome sequences of half NFLG for the two samples respectively, and they may not exhaustively capture the full profiles of the viral quasispecies. What's more, the tropism prediction is conducted using genotypic rather than phenotypic drug resistance testing, which may entail a certain risk of false negatives or false positives. Finally, while our phylogenetic clustering analysis supports the inference that the parental lineage of subtype F2 likely originated in Africa and that the CRF02_AG lineage is non-Chinese, these interpretations must be considered in light of significant limitations: (1) our analysis is constrained by sampling bias. Genomic surveillance efforts are unevenly distributed globally that could harbor unsampled diversity relevant to the origins of these lineages. (2) the incompleteness of available sequence databases could lead to incomplete or potentially misleading inferences regarding viral origins and migration pathways.

## Conclusions

In conclusion, this study revealed a URF derived from subtype F2 and CRF02_AG. The recombinant structure consisted of a subtype F2 backbone and two fragments of CRF02_AG identified among HIV-infected patients in Guangdong, China. This report is the first of a full-length genome composed of these two subtypes in China, suggesting increased HIV genetic complexity in Guangdong Province. The identification of a new recombinant form may indicate the presence and transmission of several cocirculating lineages in Guangdong, possibly contributing to the emergence of new CRFs. Meanwhile, strong associations between R5/X4 HIV-1 dual tropism and fast clinical disease progression, including significantly lower CD4 cell counts, confirm the well-characterized link between X4 HIV-1 and poorer prognosis.

**Study Objectives**
The objective of this project is to systematically extract and curate data related to HIV drug resistance from published reports. For each paper, identify and summarize information on:

1. HIV nucleotide or amino-acid sequences obtained from clinical samples, including GenBank accession numbers.
2. The populations from whom HIV sequences were obtained.
3. The clinical samples and sequencing methods used.
4. Antiretroviral \(ARV\) treatment histories of the individuals whose samples were sequenced.

**Question 1 – Does the paper report HIV sequences from patient samples?**
**Goal:** Determine whether the study generated new HIV nucleotide or amino-acid sequences, or reported lists of mutations, directly from clinical samples obtained from individuals with HIV \(ART-naïve or ART-experienced\).
**Answer “Yes” if the paper:**

- States that genetic sequencing, genotypic resistance testing, Sanger sequencing, next-generation sequencing, or single-genome sequencing was performed on clinical samples such as plasma, serum, PBMCs, proviral DNA, or dried blood spots.
- Indicates that sequencing was done on samples from patients, participants, subjects, blood donors, newly diagnosed or newly infected individuals, PLWH/PWH, or cohorts of individuals with HIV.
- States that surveillance for transmitted or acquired drug resistance was performed and generated new sequence data.
- Reports GenBank accession numbers for sequences generated in the study.

**Answer “No” if:**

- Only laboratory strains \(e.g., HXB2, IIIB, NL4-3, BAL, LAI\) or site-directed mutants were studied.
- The paper is a review or meta-analysis using sequences reported in other studies or downloaded from databases without generating new sequences.

**Question 2 – Does the paper report in vitro drug susceptibility data?**
**Goal:** Determine whether the paper quantifies HIV in vitro susceptibility to ARV drugs.
**Answer “Yes” if the paper:**

- States that phenotypic susceptibility testing, phenotypic resistance testing, or a drug susceptibility assay was performed.
- Reports IC₅₀, EC₅₀, EC₉₀, fold change in susceptibility, or similar measures.
- Describes a susceptibility assay \(e.g., PhenoSense/Monogram, Antivirogram/Virco\) or gives details on cells, drug titrations, and reporter readouts.
- Specifies the virus used for testing \(e.g., clinical isolate, site-directed mutant, virus from in vitro passage\).

Otherwise, answer “No”.

**Question 3 – Were sequences from the paper made publicly available?**
**Goal:** Determine whether newly generated HIV sequences or raw reads were deposited in public repositories \(e.g., GenBank, SRA, DDBJ, ENA\).
**Answer “Yes” if the paper:**

- Provides GenBank accession numbers \(typically two letters followed by digits\) in the Methods, Results, a Supplementary Table, or Data Availability statement.
- States that sequences have been submitted to GenBank or another public database, even if accession numbers are “pending.”
- States that raw reads are available in SRA or other sequence-read repositories.

**Answer “No” if:**

- Only accession numbers for HIV reference strains \(e.g., HXB2, NL4-3, LAI, BAL\) are given.
- No accession numbers or deposition statements are provided.
- Only accession numbers from previous studies are cited.
- The paper is a review or meta-analysis using existing sequence data.

**Question 4 – What are the GenBank accession numbers for sequenced HIV isolates?**

- If the paper reports that sequences were submitted to GenBank or another public database and provides accession numbers, extract all individual accession numbers and ranges \(e.g., FJ800379–FJ800386; GQ477441–GQ477451; KP170487\).
- Accession numbers may appear in the Methods, in a table, in Supplementary material, or in a Data Availability statement.
- If accession numbers are described but extraction is ambiguous, copy the relevant text describing the submission.

If no accession numbers are given, answer “Not reported”.

**Question 5 – How many individuals had samples obtained for HIV sequencing?**

- If the paper does **not** report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, or only compiles sequences from databases/previous studies, answer **0**.
- If sequencing or genotypic resistance testing was performed on samples or sequences from X individuals, answer **X**.
- If the paper reports X isolates/sequences from a group of patients but does not specify how many individuals contributed isolates, assume one sequence per individual and answer **X**, unless stated otherwise.
- If multiple mutually exclusive patient groups are described, sum individuals across all groups.
- If sequences were generated but the number of individuals is not reported, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 6 – From which countries were the sequenced samples obtained?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, answer **“Not applicable”**.
- Use the country or countries where samples were collected \(e.g., recruitment, enrollment, follow-up, or surveillance site\).
- If multiple countries are listed, report all.
- If samples were collected in country A and sequenced in country B, report **country A**.
- If no country information is provided, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 7 – From what years were the sequenced samples obtained?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV, answer **“Not applicable”**.
- If sample collection dates are reported \(e.g., Year1–Year2, or month/year ranges\), report the year span \(e.g., “June 2004–April 2007” → **2004–2007**\).
- If samples are listed by individual years \(e.g., 2008, 2009, 2010\), report the full span \(e.g., **2008–2010**\).
- If only months within a single year are reported \(e.g., March–September 2008\), report that single year \(**2008**\).
- If baseline sequencing corresponds to enrollment or diagnosis years, use that year range.
- If no sample-collection years are provided, answer **“Not reported”**.

**Question 8 – Were samples cloned prior to sequencing?**

- If the paper does not report HIV sequences from individuals with HIV **or** does not report in vitro susceptibility data, answer **“Not applicable”**.
- Answer **“Yes”** if:
    - The paper states that “amplicons were cloned and sequenced,” or describes use of a cloning method \(e.g., TA/Topo TA cloning\).
    - Molecular clones were sequenced.
    - Single-genome amplification or limiting dilution was performed prior to sequencing.
    - Site-directed mutagenesis was performed on isolates that were sequenced.
- Answer **“No”** if:
    - Direct PCR or population-based sequencing is reported.
    - A commercial genotyping platform \(e.g., ViroSeq, TruGene, GeneSeqR, GenoSure, Vela Diagnostics\) is used.
    - Next-generation sequencing \(NGS\) without cloning is used.

# Predicting the Impact of Drug Resistance Mutations on Inhibitor Potency with Molecular Dynamics and Machine Learning


ABSTRACT: Many enzymes are vital drug targets in diseases such as cancer and pathogenic infections; however, mutations can drastically disrupt inhibitor binding to confer resistance. Resistance mutations primarily occur at the inhibitor binding site, but accompanying distal mutations can exacerbate resistance to render even highly potent inhibitors obsolete. While structure-based analysis is often critical to drug design, the enzyme-inhibitor complex structures provide little insight as to why the mutated enzyme variant is resistant. In this study we are using a very potent inhibitor, darunavir, bound to a series of 28 variants of HIV-1 protease with affinities from picomolar to micromolar, to develop an accurate method for predicting resistance. Our optimized strategy involves rerefining cocryystal structures to ensure accurate

inhibitor geometries and combining parallel molecular dynamics simulations with feature selection to develop a robust machine learning model to predict loss of potency and resistance. The best performing models included only physics-based features of intramolecular interactions, with four specific features largely distal from the active site sufficient to predict binding affinity within 1 kcal/mol of the experimental value, far better than models based on either the structures or sequences alone. Thus, we demonstrate a strategy to robustly predict the loss of binding potency due to unseen drug-resistance mutations.

## 2. COMPUTATIONAL METHODS

The optimized strategy for determining the key predictive features of drug resistance is represented in the flowchart in Figure 1. The strategy involved curating and optimizing the starting enzyme-inhibitor molecular structure, setting up and performing parallel MD simulations, extracting the physics-and geometry-based features, dividing the data set into training and test sets, prioritizing the features with elastic net linear regression in comparison with the experimentally determined inhibition data, reducing the features and validating the resulting machine learning model. In this section we describe the optimization of the structures and methods for the optimized strategy to predict the impact of drug resistance mutations.

2.1. Preparation of Enzyme-Inhibitor Structures. Crystal structures of enzyme-inhibitor complexes, including unfortunately our own, are notorious for not retaining ideal chemical geometry of the organic small molecule ligands during refinement.[62-65] We noticed the bond lengths of bis-THF atoms in DRV were different across the protease-DRV complexes. To correct any discrepancies in the published PDB structures, we optimized the geometry of DRV and rerefined the crystal structures.
2.1.1. Geometry Optimization of DRV. Quantum mechanical (QM) geometry optimization was performed on the small molecule inhibitor DRV (structure taken from PDB ID: 6DGX). The input file was generated in GaussView  \(6^{66}\)  and QM calculations were performed using Gaussian 16 software.[67] The DRV structure was optimized using the Hartree-Fock method with the B3LYP 6-31\*G basis set.[68,69] The resulting DRV structure had subtle changes in both bond angles and bond lengths (Table S1) and was used in all subsequent crystallographic rerefinements and MD simulations. The corresponding atom indices are displayed on the DRV structure in Figure S1.
2.1.2. Refinement of DRV Cocryystal Structures. To ensure that the starting structures of HIV-1 protease-DRV complexes

All crystal waters present in the template were retained.
2.1.4. Preparation of Starting Structures. In total there were 28 HIV-1 protease variant-DRV complexes (Figure 2A) that were prepared for system building and MD simulations. The 28 variants had mutations at a total of 48 out of 99 residue positions; these include 7 positions at or near the active site (residues 32, 47, 48, 50, 82, 84), and 41 positions far from the active site (residues 7, 10, 16, 20, 30, 33, 35-37, 41, 43, 45, 46, 53-55, 58, 60-64, 66, 67, 69, 71-74, 76, 77, 85, 88-90, 93, 95) (Figure 2B and Figure S2). The number of mutations in a given variant ranged from 0 in wildtype up to 24 mutations, and the experimental enzyme inhibition constant  \((K_{\mathrm{i}})\)  values ranged from picomolar to micromolar (Figure 2A and Table S3). Although it is possible that the HIV-1 protease mutations affect the stability of native versus denatured protein, the variants used in the present study are functional, catalytically active, and can be crystallized for structure determination.[3,36-41,56-61] For each structure, PlayMolecule ProteinPrepare[73] was used to titrate protonation states and add missing atoms while optimizing the hydrogen network. To ensure consistency, the chain identifications of the two monomers

were exchanged if necessary: in all structures, chain B was in contact with the aniline moiety of DRV, while chain A was in contact with the bis-THF moiety. In all complexes, the catalytic aspartic acid of chain A was protonated.

2.2. Molecular Dynamics (MD) Simulations. MD simulations were performed using Amber 22 software,[74,75] utilizing the latest Amber force fields to ensure accurate modeling. The general Amber force field 2 (GAFF2)[76] was applied for DRV, ff19SB[77] for amino acids, with OPC water and ion parameters.[78]
2.2.1. DRV Parametrization. The partial charges of DRV were calculated by applying Antechamber AM1-BCC \(^{79}\)  charge calculations to the optimized structure of DRV. Using pharmchk2, the force field parameters for DRV were identified from GAFF2. Tleap was used to generate the library file of DRV force field parameters.
2.2.2. Preparation of MD Systems. HIV-1 protease variant-DRV systems were solvated using the OPC water model in a truncated water octahedron box ensuring at least  \(10\AA\)  between any solute atom and the periodic boundaries. The volume of the resulting box was calculated and used to estimate the number of ions needed to neutralize the system's charge and achieve a physiological concentration of  \(0.15\mathrm{M}\)  excess salt; this resulted in a total of  \(35\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\) and  \(35\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) buffer ions. Lastly, Cleap was used to generate the system topology and parameter file and system coordinate file.
2.2.3. MD Simulations. All MD simulations were performed with Amber 22 software using Particle Mesh Ewald Molecular Dynamics (PMEMD) \(^{80}\)  with the pmemd.CUDA executable on a variety of NVIDIA GPUs on the UMass Chan Medical School Scientific Computing for Innovation Cluster and the Purdue University Anvil supercomputer.
Before performing production MD simulations, the solvated system was gradually minimized and then relaxed over a series of nine steps. The initial two minimizations were performed for 1000 cycles, where the first 20 cycles utilized the steepest descent algorithm before shifting to the conjugate gradient algorithm for the remaining cycles. Each relaxation step was

run over 1 ns of simulation time. In the first step, the energy of water and ions was minimized while all other atoms were restrained. Next, the system was heated from 100 to  \(298\mathrm{K}\)  at a constant volume. In the third step, the system was relaxed at a constant pressure with a restraint weight of  \(100\mathrm{kcal / mol}\cdot \mathring{\mathrm{A}}^2\)  placed on all solute atoms and then lowered to a weight of 10 kcal/mol-Å² in the fourth step. The system was minimized through eighth steps, where the system was relaxed at constant volume with solute restraints on the backbone of the protein and DRV heavy atoms at a restraint weight of  \(10\mathrm{kcal / mol}\cdot \mathring{\mathrm{A}}^2\)  then lowered to a weight of  \(1\mathrm{kcal / mol}\cdot \mathring{\mathrm{A}}^2\)  ,and last to  \(0.1\mathrm{kcal}/\)  mol-Å². In the final step, the system was allowed to relax with no constraints.

The MD simulations were run at constant pressure of 1 bar for  \(210~\mathrm{ns}\)  at a time step of  \(0.002~\mathrm{ps}\) , with the first  \(10~\mathrm{ns}\)  discarded as equilibration and the subsequent  \(200~\mathrm{ns}\)  used for production. The Langevin thermostat and the Berendsen barostat were used, and the SHAKE algorithm was applied to all hydrogens. A nonbonded cutoff of  \(12\AA\)  was applied to calculate van der Waals and electrostatic interactions. Each HIV-1 protease-DRV complex was simulated 3 times, for a collective sampling time of  \(600~\mathrm{ns}\) .

2.3. Molecular Feature Descriptors. To quantify conformational dynamics and correlate them with experimental enzyme inhibition, molecular descriptors of dynamic protein-inhibitor and intraprotein interactions were extracted from the production trajectories. Three-dimensional coordinates from the MD trajectories were parsed using AmberTools22 cpptraj.[81] Custom bash and python scripts were developed to run the calculations, which are available in the accompanying Github repository (https://github.com/ SchifferLab/ROBUST-2025).

2.3.1. Root-Mean-Squared Fluctuations. Using cpptraj, the root-mean-squared fluctuations (RMSF) of the protein  \(C\alpha\)  atoms and inhibitor heavy atoms were calculated to assess the flexibility and dynamic behavior of these atoms over the simulation. Additionally, the root-mean-square deviations (RMSD) of the protein were calculated relative to the reference frame of the production trajectory at 20 ps intervals.

2.3.2. Calculation of Nonbonded Interactions. Pairwise van der Waals (vdW) and electrostatics (ES) interaction energies between all residue-residue and residue-inhibitor atom pairs were extracted from the production trajectory at 20 ps intervals using the pairwise function in cpptraj. The cpptraj pairwise function calculates vdW energies using the Lennard-Jones potential

\[
V (r) = 4 \epsilon \left[ \left(\frac {\sigma}{r}\right) ^ {1 2} - \left(\frac {\sigma}{r}\right) ^ {6} \right] \tag {1}
\]

where  \(V(r)\)  is the vdW potential energy,  \(\epsilon\)  is the depth of the potential well,  \(\sigma\)  is the finite distance at which the interparticle potential is zero, and  \(r\)  is the distance between the particles.

For electrostatic energies, the cpptraj pairwise function uses the Coulomb potential

\[
E _ {e l e c} (r) = \frac {q _ {1} q _ {2}}{4 \pi \epsilon_ {0} r} \tag {2}
\]

where  \(E_{elec}(r)\)  is the electrostatic potential energy,  \(q_{1}\)  and  \(q_{2}\)  are the charges of the interacting atoms,  \(\epsilon_0\)  is the permittivity of free space, and  \(r\)  is the distance between the charges.

For controls, physical features from the starting structures alone and sequence-based features were derived. For static

structure features, the pairwise nonbonded interactions were calculated on the solvated HIV-1 protease variant-DRV complexes using the vdW and electrostatic calculations described above. For sequence-based model, the amino acid sequences were converted to a binary feature vector, with a value of 0 indicating an amino acid substitution relative to NL4-3 wild type.

2.3.3. Feature Preprocessing. All calculated features were transformed to Z-scores using the equation

\[
Z = \frac {x - \mu}{\sigma} \tag {3}
\]

where  \(\mu\)  is the mean of the feature values, averaged across all frames of the three replicates.  \(\sigma\)  denotes the standard deviation calculated from the three-replicate means. Z-scores of the final test set and the cross-validation test sets were calculated by using the training set mean and standard deviation, for each feature  \(x\) . This standardization ensures that the features have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, facilitating direct comparisons and compatibility across different scales.

The pairwise vdW and ES energies were first calculated on a per-frame basis and then averaged within each replicate. The replicate feature values were concatenated into a csv file using custom bash and python scripts. The resulting replicate-level averages for each complex were subsequently averaged across the three replicates in a Jupyter notebook. The experimental potency values (Figure 2A and Table S3) were converted from  \(K_{i}\)  to  \(\Delta G\)  using the equation

\[
\Delta G = R T \ln K _ {i} \tag {4}
\]

where  \(R\)  is the gas constant (0.001987 kcal/(mol·K)),  \(T\)  is the temperature in kelvin (298 K), and  \(K_{i}\)  is the experimental inhibition constant in molar.

2.4. Feature Selection. 2.4.1. Feature Reduction. The final data set contained significantly more physical features than the number of experimental potency values. To avoid overfitting, elastic net was applied to the training data set using Python Scikit-learn \(^{82}\)  to determine the correlation coefficient for each feature. We applied an L1 ratio of 0.75, and the elastic net model was trained on  \(2/3\)  of the data. To ensure convergence of the resulting coefficients, cross-validation was performed 100 times with different permutations of the training set. All nonzero  \((p < 0.05\) , one sample  \(t\)  test) coefficients were ranked according to their mean absolute values, and a subset of seven parameters was chosen based on relative ranking

2.4.2. Feature Stability. To determine the stability of the key predictive features across different data splits, elastic net model training was repeated 100 times with different training and test splits of the data set. The correlation coefficients for each feature were compared across the different splits. The number of times each feature had a nonzero coefficient was counted, and the average coefficient across the models which include the respective feature was calculated.

2.5. Regression Analysis. 2.5.1. Model Selection. An advantage of linear regression is that the predictive variables are straightforward to interpret. We used this advantage to model the relationship of dynamics and potency, while also revealing the mechanisms by which distal mutations confer resistance. Therefore, the relationship of the  \(p\)  physical features and the  \(N\)  experimental potencies from the data set was modeled using the equation

f (X) = \beta_ {0} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {p} x \beta_ {i} \tag {5}

2.5.2. Model Evaluation. The performance of the model on the training and validation sets were evaluated using the root-mean square error (RMSE)

\[
R M S E = \sqrt {\frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \left(f (x) _ {i} - y _ {i}\right) ^ {2}} \tag {6}
\]

the Pearson correlation

\[
\rho_ {\text {P e a r s o n}} = \frac {\operatorname {c o v} (f (x) , y)}{\sigma_ {f (x)} \sigma_ {y}} \tag {7}
\]

and the Spearman correlation

\[
\rho_ {\text {S p e a r m a n}} = \frac {\operatorname {c o v} (r f (x) , r y)}{\sigma_ {r f (x)} \sigma_ {r y}} \tag {8}

where  \(N\)  is the number of data points,  \(f(X)\)  is the prediction based on the independent variables  \(x\) ,  \(y\)  is the vector of dependent variables,  \(\operatorname{cov}(f(x), y)\)  is the joined covariance, and  \(\sigma_{f(x)}\)  and  \(\sigma_y\)  are the standard deviations. In the Spearman correlation equation, the prefix "r" indicates that the continuous variables were transformed into ranks. ## 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

3.1. Molecular Descriptors Derived from MD Simulations. In developing the first iteration of our knowledge-based MD-coupled ML pipeline, we performed MD simulations for 100 ns each, which was able to generate a linear regression ML model that was sufficiently predictive of inhibitor potency. \(^{44}\)  To increase conformational sampling while maintaining computational efficiency, we doubled the simulation time to 200 ns for each replicate. We ensured that the system RMSD converged prior to the production MD run and maintained equilibrium through the entire 200 ns simulation, as displayed in Figure S3 in the Supporting Information. To characterize changes in structural dynamics across the HIV-1 protease variants, 200 ns MD simulations of all 28 HIV-1 protease variants were performed in triplicate. The system reached equilibrium prior to the 200 ns production, which was confirmed by the convergence of RMSD of the protease-DRV complexes (Figure S3). The types of molecular descriptors that can be derived from MD simulations are mainly physics-based features (e.g., vdW, ES) and geometric features (e.g., RMSF, hydrogen bond (H-bond) frequencies). A total of 3,113 nonzero physics- and geometric-based features were extracted from the production trajectories for individual inhibitor atoms and protein residues, on a residue-residue and residue-inhibitor atom basis. These features breakdown into 1,505 vdW energies, 1,038 ES, 334 H-bond frequencies, and 236 RMSF values. While initially we included all four of these feature types, we discovered that RMSF and H-bond frequencies were not selected as top features by Elastic Net, and they did not show as strong of a correlation with potency as the vdW and ES energies. Therefore, our final models only included the physics-based vdW and ES.

3.2. Elastic Net Regression Identifies Physical Features Correlated with Potency. The final data set contained 2,543 physical features, which significantly exceeded the number of experimental potency values, presenting the problem of 'large  \(p\) , small  \(n\) . To address this concern, Elastic Net regularization was applied to reduce the feature set to the key features that best describe the relationship between dynamics and binding affinity in the HIV-1 protease-DRV system. Elastic net is the preferred method for high dimensional data where there are more features than observations.[84] Furthermore, Elastic Net exhibits a grouping effect, which is advantageous when  \(\mathfrak{p} \gg \mathfrak{n}\)  because it promotes the selection of correlated variables together, rather than arbitrarily choosing one and discarding the rest, which is the case when Lasso is applied to the 'large  \(\mathfrak{p}\) , small  \(\mathfrak{n}\) ' scenario. Therefore, we applied elastic net regularized regression to identify the molecular descriptors from the MD simulations to reflect the underlying relationship between dynamics and experimental potency.

To avoid overfitting the training data, elastic net was applied to the entire set of physics-based features and experimental potencies, and the correlation coefficients were used to rank the weight of each feature in predicting potency. Using this method, 60 physics-based features were identified to have nonzero coefficients. When ranked by the mean absolute value of their coefficient, the features exhibited a decay with the elbow of the curve around 0.025 (Figure 3A). Only 7 of the features had coefficients above 0.025, and these features were chosen to further assess their predictive strength.

Significantly, all 7 selected features involved pairwise interactions between protein residues, while none of them involved interactions with the inhibitor, DRV. Four of these features were vdW contacts  \((12_{\mathrm{A}} - 13_{\mathrm{A}}, 14_{\mathrm{A}} - 65_{\mathrm{A}}, 10_{\mathrm{A}} - 82_{\mathrm{A}}, 46_{\mathrm{B}} - 53_{\mathrm{B}})\)  and the remaining three were ES energies  \((12_{\mathrm{A}} - 21_{\mathrm{A}}, 46_{\mathrm{B}} - 54_{\mathrm{B}}, 44_{\mathrm{A}} - 56_{\mathrm{A}})\) . These features are asymmetrically distributed within the homodimer; with 5 within monomer A and 2 within monomer B. Interestingly, of the residues involved in these features only  \(82_{\mathrm{A}}\)  is at the active site and contacts DRV, whereas the rest of the residues are distal to the active site. To assess the interdependence of the 7 selected features, hierarchical clustering was performed on their cross

correlation with each other (Figure 3B). This separated the 7 features into two distinct clusters that were highly intercorrelated: the first cluster containing  \(12_{\mathrm{A}} - 13_{\mathrm{A}}, 46_{\mathrm{B}} - 54_{\mathrm{B}}, 46_{\mathrm{B}} - 53_{\mathrm{B}}\)  and the second cluster containing  \(14_{\mathrm{A}} - 65_{\mathrm{A}}, 10_{\mathrm{A}} - 82_{\mathrm{A}}, 12_{\mathrm{A}} - 21_{\mathrm{A}}, 44_{\mathrm{A}} - 56_{\mathrm{A}}\)  (Figure 3B). Two features  \((46_{\mathrm{B}} - 53_{\mathrm{B}}\)  and  \(46_{\mathrm{B}} - 54_{\mathrm{B}})\)  showed a particularly strong correlation with one another, as displayed by the dark red color in Figure 3B. In some cases, the motions of neighboring residues are well correlated during MD simulations; thus, it was unsurprising to see a strong correlation between the two features that involve residue  \(46_{\mathrm{B}}\)  and neighboring residues  \(53_{\mathrm{B}}\)  and  \(54_{\mathrm{B}}\) . However, a high degree of correlation between features involving the same residue is not obligatory, as the two features that involve residue  \(12_{\mathrm{A}}\) \((12_{\mathrm{A}} - 13_{\mathrm{A}}\)  and  \(12_{\mathrm{A}} - 21_{\mathrm{A}})\)  are moderately anticorrelated with each other, as shown in Figure 3B. Taken together, these findings indicate collinearity and some redundancy among the features.

The 7 physics-based features were confirmed to be linearly correlated with experimental binding potency. We plotted the feature values versus observed binding free energy  \((\Delta G)\)  and calculated the  \(\mathbb{R}^2\)  values, which were calculated as the square of  \(\rho_{\mathrm{Pearson}}\)  and represents the fraction of the variance in experimental potency explained by the feature. (Figure S4). Two features,  \(12_{\mathrm{A}} - 3_{\mathrm{A}}\)  (Figure S4B) and  \(14_{\mathrm{A}} - 65_{\mathrm{A}}\)  (Figure S4C), displayed the strongest correlation with potency  \((\mathrm{R}^2 = 0.58\)  and 0.60, respectively). The vdW interaction between residues  \(14_{\mathrm{A}}\)  and  \(65_{\mathrm{A}}\)  showed a bimodal distribution (Figure S4C). The interaction between residues  \(14_{\mathrm{A}}\)  and  \(65_{\mathrm{A}}\)  was shown to be more favorable as DRV resistance increased. A bimodal distribution is evident in another vdW feature,  \(46_{\mathrm{B}} - 53_{\mathrm{B}}\)  (Figure S4E), but in this case we observed the interaction between residues  \(46_{\mathrm{B}}\)  and  \(53_{\mathrm{B}}\)  to be less favorable as resistance increased. From this analysis, we concluded that predictive
